To address this gap, we propose a framework that captures the concept of neighborhood fairness - a fairness criterion applicable to GNN operations. Our framework defines three types of neighborhood fairness: (i) quantifiable fairness measures; (ii) quantitative fairness optimization strategies; (iii) experimental evaluations of fairness-aware graph training methods including graph generation, graph classification and link prediction frameworks. To enable fair graph learning, we suggest two approaches: (i) graph design (redefining node labels and node affinities) and (ii) training with neighborhood fairness. Our experiments demonstrate that training with neighborhood fairness significantly improves both fairness and performance on in-domain datasets, while also leading to better generalization on out-of-domain datasets.

This research focuses on kinetic models for reversible enzyme reactions and evaluates the effectiveness of two analytical techniques in obtaining approximate solutions to these models. We apply and compare the Homotopy Perturbation Method and the Simple Iteration Method to derive approximate analytical solutions to non-linear equations describing reversible enzyme reactions.  The resulting approximations demonstrate a comparable level of accuracy.  Additionally, we use these analytical methods to investigate steady-state conditions and examine the convergence of iterative processes using Monte Carlo simulations.

Theoretical predictions of supersymmetry production are tested using data collected from 2016 proton-proton collisions at the LHC, utilizing the CMS detector's capabilities to detect final states consisting of multiple jets and large transverse momentum. With data derived from up to 35.9 inverse femtobarns of luminosity, an analysis is conducted to identify signs of supersymmetry in the context of natural and split scenarios. Since supersymmetry signals are expected to exhibit large masses and significant missing transverse momentum, an analysis is also performed to compare jet energy scale measurements against the superyttrition split scenario's predictions. With results indicating that measurements are consistent with theoretical predictions or standard model expectations, limits are placed on supersymmetry cross sections in multiple scenarios, including the framington and vanishing junction limit. With results applicable to gluino masses up to 2.1 TeV in the framington scenario and 2.3 TeV in the vanishing junction scenario, and with results also excluding a split supersymmetry model with gluino masses above 3.1 TeV for top squark masses up to 1 TeV, an analysis is conducted to test the predictions of supersymmetry in the split supersymmetry model.

Two proposed expectation models for temporary financial bubbles, involving individuals with varied predictions and positive influences, show that bubble collapse can be certain and timely. The models are tested against historical data for the 2007 bubble in the US housing market. Its similarity to the model "individual expectations with positive drift and random termination time" suggests that the bubble's collapse was likely the result of excessive speculation, and that its timing was in line with the peak of the market in late 2005.

Quantum harmonic oscillators were computationally analyzed in their ground state with either classical or quantum coercion, utilizing various approaches to derive a coherent effective Lagrangian. This effective Lagrangian was then used to determine key coordinates within the Wigner path integral. Two distinct Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods were employed: Local Metropolis and Langevin simulations. These methods were tested against exact numerical calculations, revealing that Langevin simulations provided more accurate results. Nonetheless, a Local Metropolis simulation at a higher sampling rate managed to match the accuracy of Langevin simulations, although sampling rate significantly impacted performance. Analytical approximations derived from coherent state ground states were also evaluated, demonstrating that Langevin simulations closely emulated these, particularly at high coercion strength.

Recent research has shown significant progress in improving recommender systems through data augmentation, which has become a crucial topic in NLP. These systems aim to generate comprehensive training data by synthesizing existing text examples. The existing methods in this area have primarily focused on generating pseudo-positive reviews for part-of-property (POP) items, but their performance is still subpar when confronted with real-world challenges. In this study, we present SIFN, a cutting-edge method for review-based item recommendation that tackles several pressing issues. Firstly, we aim to systematically combine review-level and aspect-level information to effectively represent each review. Secondly, we introduce a user-modeling component using user-item interaction data to capture user preferences. Lastly, we address the challenge of learning from both synthetic and real reviews in a collaborative setting. The experimental results demonstrate the superiority of SIFN over state-of-the-art methods under strict evaluation conditions, showcasing its remarkable performance on two public datasets.

Developing CS NLP systems is particularly challenging in languages that exhibit high levels of CS. This paper explores data augmentation as a solution to address the inherent biases in CS text generation. We examine the effect of substituting words with synonyms on improving data parity for Arabic-English CS data through both CS word-level and sentence-level transformations. Notably, a factor often overlooked in CS data augmentation is the impact of lexical replacements. We investigate how different types of replacement, including identity, partial, and full substitution of words, can enhance data augmentation. Our findings reveal that applying lexical replacements in conjunction with CS-based sentence reordering yields the best results, achieving 93.55% parity in men-women text generation.

We show that any subgroup of homeomorphisms of a compact surface that fix the boundary, whose action within the surface's interior is highly transitive, cannot be topologically compact when using the compact-open topology's inherited structure.

We're investigating integrable boundary conditions that can be geometrically interpreted as D-branes within specific theoretical models based on products of group- and coset-spaces, which are generalized versions of lambda deformations. Utilizing a sigma-model approach, we found that all the established conformal brane geometries in the context of products of WZW models satisfy the relevant boundary conditions, thereby maintaining their integrability across the renormalization group flow in our sigma-models. The identified brane geometries comprise traditional G-conjugacy classes, their twisted counterparts defined by the twisted conjugation induced by the automorphisms involved in the products, and more generally, hyper-Kahler quotients that apply uniformly across the above-mentioned spaces. The analysis also highlights the importance of the monodromy transparency in the fibrations of brane configurations when considering their long-term renormalization group evolution behavior.

A high-quality hexahedral mesh is often the go-to choice for simulations and analysis due to its benefits. Untangling hex meshes with large tetrahedral holes is essential for assessing their quality, but current methods have limitations. Existing hex-mesh untangling algorithms can only handle up to 32 tets or fewer than 160 tets per hex element. Building upon successful mesh deformation untangling techniques, we developed new methods to untangle large hex meshes with hundreds of tets. Our innovative methods leverage hex-element characteristics to divide the tetrational domain into smaller sub-components. By applying these new methods, we can untangle hex meshes with up to 58 tets per hex element and numerous others containing many tets. Our approach also allows for the efficient evaluation of hex-mesh quality metrics. Untangling hex meshes enables the visualization of inherent distortions resulting from deformation and evaluation of specific features, such as the symmetry of untangled hex-meshes. Our new methods facilitate the development of untangling algorithms for more complex mesh structures, like pentahedral meshes. Furthermore, we create an open-source tool to untangle hex-meshes and demonstrate its effectiveness with real-world applications, such as untangling a hex-mesh to analyze a brain CT scan with severe distortions.

The tasks of relation extraction and knowledge graph link prediction share a
common link in their objectives, allowing them to complement each other in the
process of predicting a subject-object relationship in a sentence. Specifically,
when a model identifies an object and its related subject, this relationship can
be utilized by another model to anticipate a list of potential objects associated
with the subject, indicating that the original object is also a probable choice.
In this paper, a dual-learning approach is proposed, integrating relation
extraction with knowledge graph link prediction to enhance the prediction of
subject-object relationships. The link prediction task serves as a means to
evaluate existing object choices in a sentence, resulting in notable gains in
relation extraction accuracy on various datasets.

This study introduces an innovative analytical delay model specifically tailored for deep submicron CMOS inverters. Developed based on the critical recognition that inverter delay is a complex interplay of multiple process variables and load capacitance, the proposed model incorporates parameterized equations derived using Curve Fitting Toolbox in Matlab to accurately capture these dynamics. In comparison to simulation results generated by SPICE and the BSIM4 transistor model, the analytical delay model exhibits remarkably high precision, demonstrating an average error of less than 2% across an extensive range of technological parameters and output loads. As a result, the proposed model presents itself as a computationally efficient solution for diverse technology nodes and probabilistic gate delay characterisation applications.

Making optimal decisions in complex, continuously changing environments requires
assuming certain conditions. Often, we assume a certain structure exists, but in many cases,
we can't, so we must rely on prior experience to make informed decisions. In our study,
we focus on a specific type of environment, those with a certain geometric property,
and we aim to find a way to measure how well a model predicts the outcome of a decision
by using a metric. Our work reveals that, in these types of environments, the effectiveness
of a model in making decisions is related to how closely it adheres to this metric. Furthermore,
we show that, with sufficient data, an optimal model can be identified.

The underlying mechanisms of the ventral temporal cortex's animacy organization remain contentious, suggesting that animacy exists along a spectrum rather than a binary divide. Recent evidence suggests this continuum is influenced by the degree of presence or absence of distinct animal features or by how entities are perceived as social agents. In this study, a stimulus set with independent factors of visual categorizability and agency perception in the social agent category was used to test these hypotheses in a functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) experiment. The results showed that visual categorizability, not presence or absence of animal features or agency perception in the social agent category, explained activation patterns in the lateral fusiform gyrus, a region previously implicated in the animacy organization of the ventral temporal cortex. Furthermore, multivariate analysis of posterior regions of the ventral temporal cortex revealed distinct patterns for categories of highly visible, but not featureless, animals and inanimate entities. These findings support the animacy spectrum hypothesis and provide insight into the complex nature of agency perception in the social agent category.

In scientific simulations, filtering is commonly used to stabilize computations and produce aesthetically acceptable results. However, this approach often neglects to conserve key solution characteristics. To address this issue, we have developed a new filtering technique that preserves essential properties of the simulated solution. By formulating filtering as an optimization problem with prescribed constraints, we have created an algorithm that ensures the presence of specific solution attributes in the filtered data. Our approach can be applied to a wide range of simulation types, including linear elliptic equations, and can accommodate complex geometries and non-uniform grids. Furthermore, our method's performance in reducing error and improve convergence rates in the L2 norm can be proven theoretically. To showcase its effectiveness, we have tested our approach in various real-world scenarios, including 2D and 3D benchmarks from various fields, and have observed significant improvements in the filtered data.

Quasi-periodic oscillations type C, typically observed in low-hard and hard-intermediate states of black hole X-ray transients, have been investigated using the MAXI J1535-571 data collected by Insight-HXMT. By applying a novel time-dependent Comptonization model and a relativistic reflection model, researchers have demonstrated its ability to accurately describe X-ray data up to 300 keV in the hard-intermediate state. Observations show the model naturally accounts for the evolution of the hard X-ray spectrum, corona size, and inner edge of the disk. Notably, the analysis indicates the inner edge of the disk transitions from the disk's outer boundary to the last stable orbit during the hard-intermediate state. In the soft-intermediate state, the analysis suggests the inner edge of the disk sits on the last stable orbit. By analyzing the hard X-ray spectrum with a time-dependent Comptonization model, researchers have found the corona size and flow rate change significantly, while also influencing the disk's inner edge. Furthermore, the analysis of the fluorescent spectrum allows the authors to monitor the corona size and the outer edge of the disk.

In the context of multi-agent reinforcement learning, particularly for tasks requiring cooperation and communication, MARL agents are prone to being brittle due to their potential for overfitting on the policies of their training partners. As a result, they may adapt strategies that exploit or heavily rely on the specific actions or behavior of the agents with which they are trained. To address this issue, we introduce a novel method called transfer empowerment (TEP) with the intrinsic motivation principle, which aims to encourage agents to achieve a higher level of exploration in the state-action space and acquire more general policies. TEP achieves this by incorporating an information-theoretic module that promotes behavior increasing uncertainty for the agent in question and their potential partners. By doing so, TEP empowers agents to adopt more robust policies that are less susceptible to the actions of their training counterparts. As evidence of its efficacy, we find that agents trained using TEP exhibit improved generalization to new partners, both in scenarios where the partner's behavior is fixed and when it is dynamic. Furthermore, the implementation of TEP results in successful cooperation in tasks involving communication, as well as reduced dependency on the specific training partner's actions in various competitive and collaborative settings.

We introduce MatSim, a groundbreaking synthetic dataset generated using physics-based rendering, simulating real-world material appearances under various lighting and environmental conditions. By training a neural network on MatSim, we successfully enable materials to be recognized across any given condition. MatSim promotes zero-shot or few-shot cross-domain material recognition. Unlike traditional datasets, MatSim is versatile and can be utilized for multiple applications. By training a contrastive learning algorithm using MatSim, we achieve 70%, an improvement of 13% compared to the previously most accurate model over multiple state-of-the-art techniques. Furthermore, MatSim facilitates enhanced transfer learning, resulting in an average performance boost of 5-10% compared to models trained on other materials datasets. MatSim is available at https://github.com/isa-timeflow/MatSim.

Two equivalent formulations of Lie 2-algebras are recalled: one as a categorification of Lie algebras and another as 2-term L∞-algebras. The paper proceeds by outlining the cohomology of strict Lie 2-algebras, revisits the cocycle theory of Lie 2-algebras, and briefly touches on Nijenhuis operators and multivector fields on a 10-dimensional manifold. The paper concludes by discussing 2-derivative algebras and Lie 2-superalgebras.

We introduce a novel method for local image feature matching, where instead of a sequential process, we first identify pixel-wise dense matches at a basic level and refine the good matches at a detailed level. In contrast to other dense methods, we leverage self and cross attention mechanisms in the Transformer model to derive feature descriptors that preserve long-range pixel interdependence. The dense features enable us to initially establish a wide range of candidate matches, which are then filtered and refined through a detailed analysis. The effectiveness of our approach, known as LoFTR, is demonstrated in two challenging scenarios: self-localization in outdoor environments and image registration. The results reveal that LoFTR significantly outperforms or complements existing methods, achieving a 10% higher accuracy on the self-localization benchmark and comparable or improved results on other registration benchmarks. The source code can be found at https://github.com/chriswalton/loftr.

The conversion of line-integrated magnetograms into three-dimensional vector solar magnetic field data relies on an inverse problem solution that inherently introduces bias into the resulting data. The extent of this bias varies in relation to inherent image quality, noise levels, and limitations of the employed forward models. To improve vector data derived from line-integrated magnetograms, we have developed an iterative method that recalculates the three-dimensional vector magnetic field mapping with a constraint on the inferred line-integrated magnetogram. This refinement minimizes bias in the vector data without compromising the line-integrated measurements. By applying this iterative method, we have successfully reduced bias in the vector data to nearly all types of observation scenarios, yielding significantly improved results. Specifically, our improvements have resulted in a 40% average reduction in bias when using the flow field and a 60% reduction in bias when using the mean field strength. Additionally, our iterative technique has shown to be compatible with existing noise reduction techniques, allowing for the efficient removal of noise from solar magnetic field data.

This research paper explores a real-world scenario in which consumers respond to varying electricity prices driven by substantial generation costs from renewable resources. We present a pricing mechanism, instant load billing, to mimic the effects of spot market prices on consumer behavior. We model consumers' reactions to changing instant prices as a joint problem, apply the $\alpha$-Nash equilibrium, and propose a distributed learning algorithm to reach equilibrium, ultimately improving overall system efficiency.

The generalized form of the Schwarzschild metric in Rastall theory is applied to a specific type of charged black string. By analyzing the metric in the string's central region, the authors determine the black string's energy density and pressure, subsequently using complex Einstein equations to find the Hawking temperature. They then examine the impact of charge on the thermal Breitenlohner-Ford branch, ultimately finding that the last stable mode mass remains unchanged in Rastall theory. However, taking into account the theory's gravitational corrections, the authors observe a decrease in Hawking temperature.

The results demonstrate that the power-law convergence rates in von Neumann's Ergodic Theorem for finite spectral measures are precisely the same as in the classical version of the theorem. Specifically, for a unitary system $(\mathcal{H}, \mathcal{B}, T)$ with a spectral measure $E$, the theorem establishes that for any Borel set $B$, the step-by-step operator averages $T^n$ converge strongly to $E(B)$ within the Schatten class $\mathcal{S}_p(\mathcal{H})$ at a rate of $|T^{n/n} - E(B)|_p = o(1)$ for $n \to \infty$. Moreover, for a compact abelian system $(\mathcal{H}, T)$ with a periodic spectral measure $E$, the theorem states that for any closed set $F$, the operator averages $T^n$ converge in the weak Schatten-von Neumann topology to $E(F)$ at a rate of $|T^{n/n} - E(F)|_w = o(1)$ for $n \to \infty$.

The research on extremely metal-poor stars, particularly those with metal content similar to that of the ancient stars in the Galactic Halo, is critical to understanding the early Universe's composition and formation processes. A key challenge in identifying these stars is requiring only low-quality spectra, obtained through the BP/RP telescope, which are accessible through the Gaia Data Release 2 archive. We introduce a novel method utilizing mock observations, temperature, and surface gravity estimates, along with metallicity, which are all obtainable from the archive, to identify stars with metal content below -1.0 based on luminosity, which is estimated through the parallax. We test the efficiency and precision of this approach by simulating various mock observations and discover that it can accurately predict metal-poor stars with a 75% to 100% probability up to a distance of 500 parsecs, regardless of the stellar type's spectral characteristics. This novel method is efficient, cost-effective, and serves as a starting point for searching more detailed spectroscopic databases like the HARPS or Keck archives.

This research develops a mathematical framework for assessing fire season intensity on a global scale using historical data. The objective is to create a predictive model that forecasts severity scores using real-time climate data and seasonal predictions. The model's performance is evaluated using time series analysis and forecasting techniques, incorporating variables such as temperature, humidity, and precipitation to account for local weather conditions' influence on fire intensity. The study employs Gaussian Process regression to account for the non-linear impact of climate factors and the unpredictability of local factors. The results demonstrate that Gaussian Process regression can accurately capture the non-linear relationship between climate factors and fire intensity, while also highlighting the increased accuracy of short-term predictions using exogenous climate data. However, the data on weather conditions for specific regions is found to be insufficient for assessing fire severity. The study leverages the Climate Forecasting Laboratory's Climate Prediction Network Phase 2 datasets, which provide climate predictions, to enhance short-term prediction accuracy. The results of this research can inform decision-makers in fire management by providing accurate forecasts of fire severity, enabling them to allocate resources effectively and make data-driven strategies.

We have compiled a unique dataset of 56 languages, evaluating various metrics for morphological complexity, including measures based on word order, inflectional variability, and other factors. Our analysis reveals significant correlations among these metrics across languages. To further validate these findings, we have conducted experiments using both human judgments and machine learning techniques. These results not only support the use of certain metrics as reliable indicators of complexity but also suggest that certain other metrics may not be as informative. Our research highlights the importance of a multi-faceted approach to understanding complexity, particularly in the context of low-resource languages where quantitative representations are particularly valuable.

Researchers at Sami Sami have discovered an unusual phenomenon where massive galaxies bend space-time, enabling smaller objects to bypass them. A known example is the gravitational lens effect observed in the galaxy cluster SDSS J1029+0442, where a small star passes close to a larger galaxy, resulting in a unique light path deviation. To better understand this phenomenon, scientists employed the steady-state Einstein theory, assuming that the lens's gravity mass remains constant. By combining this theory with an algorithm that calculates the critical curves of the lens, they identified the regions most susceptible to this unique effect and its limitations. Further studies compared these results to predictions based on standard Newtonian gravity and found significant differences in the locations and frequencies of these unique events. These findings suggest that an object's self-gravity mass change could substantially impact the gravitational field, potentially detecting this effect through lensing, or by observing changes in the redshift of distant galaxies.

This research focuses on reducing the complexity of parametric partial differential equations (PPDEs) by finding an accurate approximation space for the solutions of the equations. Given incomplete information, we use two primary sources: initial assumptions about the solutions and partial measurements from the equations. Based on these sources, we have developed methods to generate effective approximation subspaces and analyzed their performance. By identifying the optimal performance limit and designing efficient ways to reach it, we establish the value of these methods for reducing the computational cost of solving the equations.

This research proposes a computing model-based approach to Independent Component Analysis, offering a closed-form algebraic method that surpasses numerical algorithms in speed. The algorithm in question is derived from a specific case of a particular type of matrix analysis, and it is shown that this particular case has unique properties that enable the decomposition of a matrix. The speed advantage of the proposed algorithm is demonstrated through a comparison of its runtime with traditional ICA methods applied to speech and music datasets.

Identifying trending social media events in real-time is crucial for various purposes, yet determining the authenticity of events described in informal online posts poses a significant challenge. Existing techniques primarily focus on detecting events from individual platforms, but the nature of social media data necessitates the analysis of both spatial and temporal data. This paper introduces an innovative method for identifying authentic spatio-temporal events on social media, using geotagged posts. It combines statistical patterns in events with cognitive approaches to filter noisy data. For efficient real-time processing, the proposed method utilizes a two-layered architecture, incorporating a distributed data relaxation system and an interactive user interface. The approach is demonstrated with two real-world scenarios: a severe storm in Italy and an earthquake in Japan.

We establish the optimal Lipschitz regularity of very weak solutions for the measure-valued elliptic PDE $-\mathrm{div}(A(x) \nabla u) = Q \; \mathcal{H}^{n-1} \llcorner \Gamma$ within a smooth domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^n$. Here, $\Gamma$ represents a $C^{1, \alpha}$-smooth hypersurface, with $Q \; \mathcal{H}^{n-1} \llcorner \Gamma$ denoting a $\mathcal{H}^{n-1}$-measure on $\Gamma$. Furthermore, the coefficient matrix $A(x)$ is defined as a symmetric, uniformly elliptic tensor with $A \in C^{0, \alpha}(\Gamma)$, and $Q \in L^1(\Gamma)$.

Advanced permanent magnets made from rare earth metals have a number of applications, including use in direct current motors and generators. Research into cobalt-rich compounds within the yttrium-cobalt-boron system has yielded several cobalt-rich YCo$_{13}$-based compounds, which exhibit magnetic properties similar to those of Fe$_{84}$Nd$_{8}$B$_{8}$.

In the field of display advertising, real-time bidding has become the standard practice. Every ad impression resulting from a query to a demand-side platform is considered a multi-armed bandit task. The key challenge here involves striking a balance between maximizing conversions and keeping costs manageable, as the optimal strategy for boosting conversion rates may lead to excessive spending and poor return on investment. This paper addresses the issue by adapting the Efron-Birnbaum theorem to display advertising to develop a sequential decision-making method that adjusts bidding strategies in real-time for optimal results. The proposed method enables the advertiser to dynamically balance the expected cost and convergence rate of convergence. Theoretical justifications and simulations demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach.

Nonclassical properties in continuous-variable quantum systems are often marked by quantum correlations and Wigner negativity. This study explores how these two nonclassical traits are connected in the context of quantum steering, a phenomenon where measurement on one system induces nonclassical phenomena in another. Investigating both quantum steering inequalities and Wigner negativity, our results demonstrate that certain quantum steering inequalities can serve as indicators for Wigner negativity and that this relationship relies heavily on specific quantifiers of quantum steering. Furthermore, our research shows that different steering inequalities are linked to Wigner negativity through common criteria, such as conditional entropy and nuclear norm. These findings provide insight into how quantum steering inequalities and Wigner negativity interrelate.

Accurate secure data analysis in quantum key distribution relies on a crucial aspect known as quantum secure data storage. Researchers have proposed a method of non-uniform random seed generation for privacy amplification in quantum key distribution. Our study focuses on understanding the effect of this non-uniform random seed on quantum secure data storage. Given that quantum secure data storage is heavily reliant on the entropy of the raw data, we have developed a method to estimate raw data entropy through a random non-uniform vector. This approach can be applied in practical quantum key distribution scenarios, offering valuable insights for secure data storage analysis.

This research paper confirms that certain types of curves, specifically those in higher dimensional space, do not fit the classification of Bertrand curves except in two-dimensional Euclidean space. A new category, called the timelike (1,3)-Bertrand curve, is defined to fill this gap and its characteristics are identified for curves in a four-dimensional Euclidean space.

We're examining the diffusion process described by the equation $u_t(t, x) = \kappa \frac{\partial}{\partial x} u(t, x) + \sigma^2 \frac{\partial^2}{\partial x^2} u(t, x)$, where both $\kappa$ and $\sigma$ are negative, with initial conditions $u(0, x) = \delta(x) + v_0(x)$. Here, $\delta(x)$ represents the Dirac delta function, and $v_0(x)$ is a continuous, bounded function. The goal is to understand how two random samples of size $N$ taken from this distribution coalesce when taken to the interval $[0, 1]$. In our work, we derive the probability that the samples do not coalesce, and create a corresponding probability measure known as the 'disjoint' distribution $\mathbb{P}_{N, 0}$. We also show that the distribution of samples taken from $u(t, x)$ converges towards $\mathbb{P}_{N, 0}$ as $t \to \infty$. Furthermore, we've established relationships between the distribution of samples and the properties of Feller diffusions. Specifically, we've identified sampling distribution limits, as well as conditions under which these limits are unique.

In this work, we explore diagrammatic methods in waveguide QED systems with a particular focus on systems utilizing delayed coherent quantum feedback. By using a specific mathematical approach within the rotating wave approximation, we demonstrate that N-photon scattering matrices in single-qubit systems can be expressed as a combination of (N-1) photon effective vertex functions and self-energy processes. This method is applicable to free quantum states and can be applied to various waveguide QED systems, including those with spontaneous emission and phononic systems, to predict the scattering responses of multi-photon states. This technique is expected to be a versatile tool for understanding and predicting the scattering responses of quantum systems in the context of waveguide QED.

A potential way to study low-mass dark matter is by utilizing boosted dark matter, taking advantage of a larger cross-section. In this study, we examine the spin-dependent scattering of boosted dark matter off target nuclei, specifically considering fermi gases as a target. We find that, given suitable boost velocities, scattering cross-sections can be increased up to 3 orders higher than suppressed SI limits. Furthermore, we discuss detection challenges and possible strategies to overcome them.
This note employs Faulhaber's Formula to elucidate why odd Bernoulli numbers equate to zero.

Continuous phase modulation detection using conventional differential detection techniques is widely employed in various communication systems. Despite its simplicity, choosing the optimal value for the differential section delay is a complex task. Research has established that the performance of the system is directly influenced by the autocorrelation and cross-correlation functions of the constellation symbols. In this paper, the impact of the conventional differential detection delay on the detection method's spectral properties and bit error rate is investigated. A cost function is introduced to optimize the detection delay, influencing both the autocorrelation and cross-correlation functions. Optimizing the delay using this method results in improved error rates for a variety of popular CPM signals.

A prominent paradigm in reward learning utilizes human feedback via comparative evaluations, but their broader adoption is hindered by the expense and labor intensity of these comparisons. To overcome this limitation, we propose grouping multiple comparisons together and allowing human labelers to mark sub-regions of a condensed representation of the groups, thereby efficiently leveraging human time. Through data visualization techniques, we generate the representation of the groups, thereby facilitating easy labeling. Our method can then efficiently rank and approximate the value of the resulting regions. Experimental results using AirSim and MuJoCo environments demonstrate that our approach significantly reduces human labeling time by at least tenfold, while also introducing minimal bias. Moreover, we find that our region-finding technique is versatile and can be applied in different human feedback scenarios, leading to time-saving gains.

We're exploring nucleon structure functions within noncommutative space-time, with the aim of gaining insight into nucleon part composition. The noncommutativity of space and time influences the noncommutative gluon field operators in a specific way, leading to modifications in gluon structure functions. These modifications are mirrored in nucleon structure functions, as revealed by a particular twist. The effects of noncommutativity are found to rise with energy and proportional to $x$. While the general form of nucleon structure functions remains unaffected, their coefficients change based on noncommutativity parameters. The analysis also uncovers how noncommutativity impacts the distribution of nucleon quark and gluon separable parts.

In typical topological systems, significant disruptions trigger a phase shift, but we've developed an adjustment to a established quantum fracture model that prevents this overload response. This adaptation results in a more complex phase structure, incorporating both a phase shift and a topological transition at a critical point. Furthermore, our analysis reveals the presence of a specific boundary state, known as a topological line, that can exist within this system. This state features collective modes behaving as gapless one-dimensional topological modes at the critical point, as well as a topological bulk gap. We've identified a specific mechanism by which this state can emerge from the system's quantum fracture definition, which also influences the associated correlation functions. This investigation also demonstrates that the topological line can be reduced to a conformal field theory of complexity, which may potentially be used in the near future in studies of topological systems.

We investigate the eigenspectra of large, randomly structured Hermitian matrices, incorporating a finite-rank deformation whose elements are uncorrelated. The eigenspace counts are found to align with those of the corresponding classical model up to a specific margin of error, for any given matrix size. The accuracy of this approximation was previously verified through numerical simulations. This work represents an extension of prior research focusing on the Schrödinger operator and the eigenspace counts of non-Hermitian matrices.

Recent advancements in dialogue tasks have been achieved through pre-trained language models. However, models reliant on surface-level dialogue text struggle to comprehend dialogue context, particularly in extracting the underlying semantic meaning. In an effort to bridge this knowledge gap, we introduce the use of Abstract Meaning Representation as a means of pre-training language models with explicit semantic information, which captures the essence of dialogue during the pre-training phase. Building upon the standard pre-training framework, we formulate a semantic-based pre-training approach that includes three key tasks: learning core semantic units, semantic-encyclopedic relations, and core semantic features of the main idea. Empirical results from the analysis of casual and task-based conversations demonstrate the superiority of our proposed model. Moreover, our experiments show that AMR-based semantic representation excels over alternative semantics like semantic parses and syntactic tree structures.

To establish trust and reduce reliance on misleading models, there is an urgent need for simple and clear machine learning algorithms.  Evaluating the simplicity of these algorithms poses a significant challenge, as conventional metrics fall short in capturing human understanding.  This work establishes a comprehensive framework for measuring interpretability by incorporating how humans learn a particular algorithm.  We have developed a new metric, the Cognitive Complexity Learning Score (CCLScore), which assesses the ease of learning an algorithm based on two key factors: the linear relationship between model complexity and learnability, and the rate of learning progression.  The CCLScore is utilized to evaluate and compare various classification algorithms, with results indicating that decision trees possess the highest level of cognitive interpretability among the examined models.

Anomaly detection without labeled data is a highly relevant problem in various fields. Many anomaly detection algorithms have been proposed in recent years, but they often require a significant amount of data. One such algorithm that has shown promise under limited label availability and small data sizes is the Isolation Forest. However, even this efficient algorithm can be optimized further, and our research aims to enhance it by integrating it with weakly supervised learning methods. Leveraging transfer learning to reduce computational costs, we have developed a new Isolation Forest called TiWS-iForest, which significantly outperforms the current state-of-the-art by achieving a 26.6% faster execution speed. Additionally, by using the anomaly score as a weak signal, we have created a boundary recognition method that improves the anomaly detection performance by 9.6% and 11.9% in two scenarios.

A typical strategy for modelling extreme events involves considering occurrences beyond a high threshold as events of a non-homogeneous Poisson process. This method has an underlying parameterisation that links the events' intensity to the threshold. However, traditional parameterisation used in extreme value theory has drawbacks, such as non-physical outcomes and complexities in simulation and inference processes. We suggest an alternative parameterisation based on quantile functions, which addresses these issues and facilitates more efficient computation and Bayesian inference for the associated probability distribution.

This analysis explores a technique for managing statistical variations in the analysis of particle collisions. We identify stationary states in the distribution of cross-sectional area, which act as centers of constant average cross-sectional area, and investigate the conditions necessary for their occurrence. The stability of these stationary states is also examined. It's been found that regions with fluctuating cross-sectional area can develop near areas of constant cross-sectional area, leading to a distinct type of phenomenon not previously documented in the field. The identified stationary states and corresponding region patterns represent a generalized application of the methods used in [arXiv: 2101.11719].

The development of large commonsense knowledge graphs has improved knowledge representation and facilitated various downstream applications remains a pressing issue due to the limitations of existing graphs. This paper describes the comprehensive update of COMET-ATOMIC, a major commonsense relation extraction dataset, significantly expanding its scope and quality with an emphasis on high-quality data, thereby enhancing the accuracy of extraction. Comparing state-of-the-art machine learning models, the updated dataset demonstrates superior conceptual and relational understanding. The updated COMET-ATOMIC 201-202 dataset is now available online.

We present the data processing pipeline developed for the Hi-GAL survey. This critical component is an integral part of the Herschel satellite project that's mapping the Galactic plane's inner regions. Leveraging a combination of Herschel Interactive Standard Environment capabilities and new, custom-designed tools, our pipeline effectively handles data reduction tasks. These include accurate data filtering, noise assessment, and efficient map generation, which utilizes a modified version of the HECA algorithm. Our pipeline's performance is extensively evaluated through a variety of tests that demonstrate its effectiveness. Maps produced using the pipeline are then released as part of the Herschel satellite project data archive.

A recent photometric study of first-generation stars in the globular cluster NGC 2808 suggested the presence of multiple populations with different metal compositions. We performed an accurate spectral analysis of nine bright stars within the cluster to determine their chemical makeup, and our findings align with the initial photometric results, indicating the existence of two distinct metal populations. We also explored other elements such as nitrogen and found higher values in the low-metal stars, consistent with evolutionary patterns. Our analysis further supports the cluster's multiple-metal populations with a ratio of high-to-low metal stars near 2:1 and challenges a prior hypothesis suggesting the absence of low-metal stars in the cluster.

To facilitate a deeper understanding of one-dimensional physical systems, we consider a simplified single file model. We derive an analytical solution for the complete first exit time statistics of an overdamped single file with absorbing boundary conditions, after which we apply these findings to investigate the speed-accuracy relationship, examining how this property is influenced by the mean squared displacement and the entropic repulsive forces within the system.

Quantum Mechanics contradicts the universally assumed, classical cause-and-effect relationship established by Reichenbach's common cause principle. This paper presents an example demonstrating that quantum effects, similar to those seen in Einstein's polarisation filter experiment, necessarily lead to situations where the common cause principle is violated. The study further validates the consistency of a previously proposed quantum equivalent of Bayes' Rule, which is based on quantum postulates, and shows that it remains consistent even in the presence of such quantum effects.

We initially report findings regarding corrections to system size for the state equation, trace anomaly, and speed of sound, using two specific theoretical frameworks: a model for massless scalar fields and another based on quenched QCD, both applying periodic boundary conditions. Additionally, we share ongoing results involving the application of Dirichlet boundary conditions to quenched QCD.

In this brief communication, we present a novel proof that utilises a recent discovery by McCarthy to demonstrate the existence of a non-trivial element within the Hn(BR, BR), where n is greater than or equal to 3, and BR denotes the Steenrod algebra. Our approach builds upon a long-standing open problem first introduced by Wang in the 1960s.

Astronomers observing celestial objects ultraviolet (UV) wavelengths are hindered by Lyman-alpha radiation, which overwhelms sensors and distorts signal readings. Although Lyman-alpha filters can mitigate this issue, they previously compromised image quality by limiting the field of view and increasing noise. We've developed a new prototype Lyman-alpha filter, which significantly improves upon existing technology by expanding the field of view to 2.8 times the size, reducing edge effects, and enhancing sensitivity. Our innovative design combines advanced materials and manufacturing techniques, which also enable high-resolution photometric capabilities across a broader range of UV wavelengths.

Optimal distributed controller design for Graph Symmetric Systems is a key focus, despite optimal feedback design being impossible without direct access to system states, due to state observation constraints. This study proposes a innovative solution by leveraging graph filter technology to design an effective and distributed controller that achieves optimal performance. Building upon recent technological breakthroughs in frequency-domain methods and large data processing capabilities, our approach translates traditional optimal problems into new forms amenable to efficient numerical solutions. Our results, combined with the widespread availability of efficient graph filter implementations, present a cutting-edge and practical solution to this critical problem, previously unsolved in the field.

Image search algorithms that retrieve and identify copied images from large databases comprise two main components: a neural network that converts an image into a transformation-resistant vector, and a high-performance but error-prone search engine that quickly matches input vectors with stored images. To optimize overall performance, we've implemented a new intermediate step where the ordering of images to be searched is altered based on the confidence levels of the network's predictions. Specifically, we've arranged the images in the database according to the network's estimated certainty, placing the most confident guesses first. This simple modification substantially boosts the speed and efficiency of image search algorithms. We've tested the technique on a massive dataset of over 200 million images and observed a 20% to 50% reduction in the average time it takes to locate a matching image copy, ultimately enabling faster and more repeatable image search iterations.

This study verifies the feasibility of using wireless transmission patterns, also known as wireless channel attributes, to authenticate data packets without relying on pre-shared keys within noisy communication environments. By analyzing data packets' phase shifts, the receiver can determine whether the packets originated from an authorized user. While this method necessitates users acquiring knowledge of each other's transmission delays and initial phase settings, it provides an additional authentication mechanism in scenarios where established encryption methods fall short, such as in post-quantum authentication settings. Furthermore, the research explores the trade-offs between the level of authentication security and encoding efficiency.

We examine smooth trajectories of particles in washboard potentials, with periodic force F = A sin(x). The particles move under the influence of this force and friction, given by F_d = -β v. The goal is to determine how velocity dispersion ε(τ) changes over time for a particle group starting at positions u0, with initial velocities in a Gaussian distribution. The change in dispersion is analyzed under different force parameters A and friction strength β. For small friction, a transition similar to the standard diffusion process occurs, with dispersion increasing linearly. For high friction, a plateau is reached where dispersion no longer increases. The found formulas can serve as a approximation for arbitrary system evolutions, with the exception of dispersion peaks.

This paper presents an adaptable, localized predictive technique that builds upon Jord\'a's (2005) model, expanding it to a non-statistical setting through the incorporation of Bayesian Additive Regression Trees. Simulation tests reveal that our novel BART-LP model successfully captures the complexities present in the impact responses of various stimuli. An initial case study indicates that, in the context of the US, the effects of shocks on the GDP are more pronounced in the event of financial crises.

We investigate the influence of the electromagnetic quantum vacuum on the angular momentum of a charge q moving in a uniform magnetic field. The orbital angular momentum generated is due to the scattering of photons from the vacuum, and its total value for a single photon exchange is calculated both analytically and semantically within the minimal coupling and Landau non-relativistic regimes. The results demonstrate that the orbital angular momentum of the photon is not divided equally between the charge q and the magnetic field; instead, some of the orbital angular momentum remains with the photon. The orbital angular momentum of the photon is dictated by the z-component orbital angular momentum of the charge q, and this phenomenon constitutes an instance of the orbital angular momentum paradox. The orbital angular momentum of the photon can be expressed using two distinct approaches - Poincaré symmetry or Wigner transformation - which yield consistent outcomes.

The primary goal of Fine-Grained Named Entity Typing (FG-NET) is to accurately identify and classify various named entity types in unstructured text, such as people, organizations, locations, etc., with a high degree of precision. In this study, we present a novel approach called FGNET-RH that can learn complex relationships between entity types, including rare and unknown types, by utilizing a two-phase process. During the initial phase, a hyperbolic neural network is trained to predict a lower-dimensional representation for each entity type, while a refinement module is employed in the second phase to iteratively update the representation of entity types based on their interconnections. Experimental results demonstrate that FGNET-RH outperforms existing methods by a significant margin on multiple datasets, including the PanX dataset enhanced with rare entity types.

This paper establishes upper limits on the Hankel determinants for the $H_2(3)(f)$ and $H_2(4)(f)$ special types, specifically within the univalent function class and the $\mathcal{U}$ class defined by a specific condition involving functions that are analytic in the unit disk $\mathbb{D}$, with normalization where $f(z)=z+a_2z^2+\cdots$.

Achieving efficient and sustainable operation in cloud data centers largely depends on virtualization technology.  To prevent overutilization of data center resources and guarantee QoS for critical applications, virtualization technology incorporates a feature that allows reserved virtual machines to access a guaranteed share of resources.  To avoid underutilization, the remaining data center resources are allocated to non-reserved virtual machines on a best-effort basis.  This paper focuses on the problem of scheduling reserved and non-reserved virtual machines to optimize data center resource utilization.  It proposes a load balancing approach, called Prepartition, to achieve this goal.  In the pre-processing phase, Prepartition analyzes the requirements of reserved virtual machines and identifies their resource needs.  It then partitions the data center into distinct sub-clusters, each with sufficient resources to accommodate the needs of multiple reserved virtual machines.  Next, Prepartition maps the reserved virtual machines to their respective sub-clusters and schedules them for execution.  To optimize data center resource utilization, Prepartition achieves equal partitioning of data center resources among sub-clusters and places non-reserved virtual machines within these partitions.  Experimental evaluation demonstrates that Prepartition achieves better resource utilization than traditional approaches for 2-10 reserved virtual machines in a 26-switch data center setup.

In modeling systems of rival agents as games, assuming each party makes rational decisions, the probable outcomes can be identified as equilibrium points. However, in scenarios where data is available but not explicitly known, direct estimation of these equilibria is challenging. A new class of neural networks, the Fixed Point Network (FPN), is capable of parameterizing maps with a fixed point property, thus enabling the prediction of equilibria. FPNs maintain the capability to optimize their weights during training, similar to standard neural networks. We establish the theoretical foundation for FPNs by proving the existence and unique solutions to the ordinariness equation, as well as the existence of FPNs for various types of equilibria. Moreover, our study demonstrates that FPNs can achieve generalization over seen and unseen games, and provides a metric to evaluate the convergence rate of an ordinariness preserving sequence. Finally, our empirical analysis across multiple domains confirms FPNs' capacity to predict equilibria, while also offering insights for fixed point-based machine learning approaches.

This study tackles the issue of assessing causal influences in cases where some variables involved in ensuring causal validity are incompletely known. For these situations, we develop tight limits on the causal influences by solving two intricate optimization problems. The derived limits prove to be sufficient, leading us to introduce an optimization technique for assessing causal influences. This method leverages optimization to solve the causal influence assessment problem even when the underlying data is high-dimensional. Importantly, our approach ensures that our solutions to this problem remain relevant even in cases where the causal influence value itself exceeds 1 (a situation known as the one-half problem).

A critical challenge in cyber-physical systems is non-intrusive, real-time detection of stealthy cyber attacks that manipulate sensors to deceive humans and disrupt system operation. This is particularly difficult in systems modeled by linear time-invariant equations, where attack effects often overlap with normal system behavior. Our research introduces a novel predictive monitoring approach, using data from informed informative attack scenarios to identify stealthy cyber attacks. This method relies on an online linear regression technique to calculate precise sensor readings and detect unusual deviations within a statistically determined threshold. Our results demonstrate that this method can effectively detect a range of attack scenarios, outperforming existing state-of-the-art approaches.

A precise summary can be derived from lengthy written documents through graph-based algorithms, which analyze the interconnection between sections. Indian languages present a special challenge for machine-based summarization due to their grammatical complexity and diverse sentence structures, making it particularly difficult to create effective algorithms. This research proposes GAE-ISumm, a program that generates summaries for texts written in Indian languages by converting the document into a graph and applying algorithms to identify key sections. Our study evaluates the effectiveness of various techniques, including machine learning models and phrase ranking, using datasets in five different languages and compares the results with a range of unsupervised and supervised systems.

We establish the definition and certain attributes of S-rings of Krull type, in addition to examining the properties of such structures, particularly independent S-rings of type A. We calculate the injective dimension of a quotient category formed by modules over an independent S-ring of type A, with respect to a specified subcategory consisting of modules having trivial interactions with codivisorial modules.

Recent advances in deep generative models using variational stochastic
sampling offer a way to learn a posterior distribution in their own right. 
Variational autoencoders are commonly used for this purpose, but learning a 
proper posterior is essential in many applications. Typically, a prior 
distribution is specified, and an objective function minimizes a loss 
measured by the Kullback-Leibler divergence of the learned distribution relative 
to the true posterior. However, previous investigations have shown that 
concentrating solely on the VAE objective can result in a posterior that is 
not representative of the data. This paper presents a new approach called 
LSVBAE, combining a regularized objective function with a least square 
optimization to accurately learn a posterior distribution. The function aims 
to minimize the least square error of the log probability density of the data 
given the prior distribution. The results of our simulations indicate that LSVBAE 
achieves better generalization performance than VAE-based approaches.

Smart home technology is gaining momentum, driven by IoT, yet it also invites cyber threats that necessitate robust and cost-effective security measures. This research contributes to filling this need by designing an affordable, network security system utilizing a private blockchain and a location tracking technique based on wireless signal strength. Our investigation highlights the benefits of private blockchains, particularly their adaptability, security, data integrity, and privacy features. This study also examines the application of wireless localisation, focusing on determining the home router's position, by analyzing and integrating the signal strength of wireless devices. The proposed approach includes developing a private blockchain-based smart home system and evaluating the effectiveness of two different localization methods, including k-Nearest Neighbors and Support Vector Machine. The findings demonstrate that the use of wireless localisation can accurately detect and identify intruders, thereby preventing cyber threats.

A novel approach to quantizing log-likelihood ratio storage utilizing deep learning has been developed for gray-coded modulations. This method requires replacement of traditional LR storage in coherent receivers equipped with conventional modulators to take advantage of its benefits. It's estimated that the suggested technique achieves a reduction in power consumption of at least 25% compared to standard storage methods, while maintaining performance through error-free decoding. Furthermore, the proposed approach allows for substantial reduction in storage precision, specifically down to 3 bits per LR, resulting in around 75% decrease in power consumption with only slight performance degradation. Our results indicate that the proposed quantizer outperforms traditional maximum a posteriori probability and minimum mean squared error receivers in various scenarios.

We have devised three new parameterized algorithms for identifying whether a directed graph can be converted into an upward planar layout. Each of the discovered parameterizations yields a specific complexity analysis: when the focus is on the number of source vertices, the problem's complexity is reduced to class $W[1]$ with a specific parameterization; when the focus is on the number of sink vertices, the problem's complexity is reduced to class $W[1]$ with a different parameterization; when the focus is on the graph's edge density, the problem's complexity is reduced to XP with a specific time complexity analysis. This research is further supported by a newly discovered NP-completeness proof for checking if a directed graph can be converted into an $\alpha$-approximate upward planar layout with a specific number of source vertices.

Crowdsourced image datasets contaminated with noise are explored, and a computer vision model's resilience to noise in classification tasks is analyzed.  A novel method for evaluating and handling noisy data points in supervised learning environments is presented.  Specifically, a neural network ensemble is trained to mitigate the effects of noise, and a specialized 'Human Softmax' distribution is developed to quantify the reliability of each data point.  Uncertainty is measured using the entropy of the 'Human Softmax' distribution and the entropy of the network's output, and a method for removing noisy data points based on these entropic measures is discussed.  A method for estimating the proportion of noisy data points through sample entropy is also presented, and this value is used to identify and remove noisy data points.  This method is applied to the NIST 19-6 dataset, and a comparison of the network's performance in single-shot and ensemble settings is presented, demonstrating the network's ability to mitigate noise and achieve superior results in supervised learning environments corrupted with noise.

For semiflows with uniformly or nonuniformly expanding dynamics, which exhibit exponential decay in correlations, we can prove the exponential decay in the H\"older norm of the transfer operators acting on smooth observables.

A particular matrix known as a covering array is constructed by combining rows of distinct non-negative integers, each representing a specific profile of certain properties. Determining the minimum number of rows required in an array of a certain size, with a certain level of consistency, is known as a covering array problem and can be quantified using the function $CA(\vec{m},k,\lambda)$, which represents the optimal number of rows needed. In this study, we examined the properties of small covering arrays of strength 2 and, by doing so, solved the function's values for the integers 1 through 11 and established a lower bound for all integers up to 11.99, which is remarkably close to the established bounds for these values.

Nonlocal games involve two players who make decisions based on random questions drawn from a set $A$, given that they share resources like entangled pairs or classical information. It has been demonstrated that players who share a resource, whether it's entangled or classical, must adhere to specific constraints when participating in nonlocal games, with violators experiencing penalties according to specific conversion rates. This study examines the decidability of ascertaining whether players who share maximally entangled sources are capable of completing nonlocal games, with violators experiencing penalties within certain ranges. It has been found that for nonlocal games with a limited number of questions, determining the exact nature of their violation, including whether it's zero or a specific minimum value, is always feasible, with the possible exception of games involving highly complex questions and high levels of noise. This study employs a new approach, by first converting a game into an equivalent game that utilizes a specific type of resource, by simplifying a different model of computation, and by applying concepts from computational complexity.

This study seeks to accurately and thoroughly document the application of a guided genetic algorithm in reproducing software crashes, building upon a previous conference paper that introduced the concept. Our work meticulously outlines each step of the algorithm and explores the challenges associated with reproducing crashes, examining the time complexity of the method's inner loop. In addition, we examine the viability of the genetic algorithm as a binary search method.

The vortex lattice in type-II superconductors exhibits triangular, square, ice-like structures before melting into liquid-like states. While the triangular and ice configurations are well-documented, the square structure has only been observed under extreme conditions, such as in extremely high magnetic fields and at low temperatures. Our study reveals the square structure in the strongly anisotropic superconductor YBa$_{2}$Cu$_3$Mo$_6$ under vortex densities and temperatures where the usual triangular and ice phases are expected. A novel square-to-square phase transition is observed, which is discovered to be pressure-tunable and involves a competition between electromagnetic and thermal interactions. This transformation can be explained by the adaptation of ice-order within the vortex lattice, indicating a multi-component order parameter. This research contributes to the understanding of the complex vortex-lattice structure and temperature-dependent phase transitions in superconducting materials.

Photons are valuable tools used to explore the early stages of heavy ion collisions (HICs) because they interact minimally with the quark-gluon plasma (sQGP) formed in these collisions. The flow of photons in these events provides a way to investigate the properties of the sQGP. Studies of photon flow can be combined with that of charged particles to determine the ratio of diagonal to orthogonal anisotropic flow parameters (v_1 / v_2) for photons. This ratio is found to be greater for photons than for charged particles. The anisotropic flow of photons is influenced more by the initial conditions of the non-flow photons than by the transport properties of the sQGP. A calculation using the ideal hydrodynamic model shows that the anisotropic flow of photons is a sensitive indicator of the viscosity-to-entropy ratio (η/s) when the hydrodynamic expansion time is short. The ratio v_1 / v_2 for photons is found to decrease as η/s increases, with similar behavior observed in the anisotropic flow of particles. The anisotropic flow of photons may provide a way to explore the viscosity of the sQGP without being affected by its thermal conductivity. This makes photon anisotropic flow a useful tool for exploring the properties of the sQGP.

Our study centers on investigating the regular magnetic order (RMO) for certain spin models with global spin rotations symmetries, focusing on group theoretical methods for triangular and kagome lattices. These regular magnetic orders hold significance as potential ground states for various spin models, making them prime candidates for study. By adhering to a framework developed by Messio et al., we extended their initial approach to incorporate kagome lattices in this current work. Key outcomes include describing all regular magnetic orders resulting from finite group subgroups of $Z_p$, classifying them as non-subgroup cases or extra orders. Notably, our findings reveal a particular class of RMOs possessing larger energies than the generic $Z_p$-subgroup cases, with these extra orders exhibiting a crucial property - irreversibility. This work aims to provide a comprehensive reference manual for classifying regular magnetic orders associated with spin-1/2 Heisenberg models featuring global spin rotations of order p.

Large data-driven companies have shifted away from traditional feature-based testing, instead focusing on extensive treatment effect assessments. This shift is driven by the desire for controlled false discovery rates, especially in situations where non-independent discoveries occur. We present an innovative approach called CEFT, an online and control-fdr conscious algorithm designed for large online testing scenarios, allowing for simultaneous detection of both positive and negative treatment effects. This method can be used at various levels of dependency and our method's performance is comparable to the currently best-known controlled fdr methods.

The foundational aspects of cosmological inflation are addressed. The derivation of equations governing the inflaton field, an introduction to slow-roll parameters, and a description of how inflationary perturbations correspond to cosmic microwave background temperature fluctuations are presented.

The CDF II experiment's recent measurement of the W boson mass, 13.0766 GeV/c^2, deviates from the Standard Model's prediction by 4.2 sigma. Combined with the Fermilab ATLAS and CMS measurements of the muon's anomalous magnetic moment, the type-X 2HDM is explored as a potential solution. A novel type-X 2HDM is introduced with a different setup of lepton-lepton and quark-quark interactions than the conventional type-X models. This include interactions such as $l^\pm l^\pm \phi$ and $q^\pm q^\pm \phi$. By examining mass generation mechanisms for the lepton and quark sectors, it is found that the type-X 2HDM, with a correctly aligned Higgs vacuum expectation value, can simultaneously satisfy the requirements for the W boson mass, muon's anomalous magnetic moment, and lepton-physics constraints like MEG.
