Software developers who perform maintenance tasks encounter multiple change requests 
submitted by software system users, presenting the difficulty of choosing suitable 
search terms for concept location during maintenance activities. A proposed technique 
QUICKAR leverages the knowledge gathered from the crowd-sourced knowledge base - 
StackExchange - to provide reformulated query options derived from related terms 
obtained from the same knowledge base. By comparing various query reformulation techniques, 
the study demonstrates the effectiveness of using StackExchange as a knowledge source, 
and demonstrates its benefits through an experiment using maintenance activity change requests.

Adaptive synchronization in interactions, or entrainment, occurs when interlocutors converge in behavioral patterns or acoustic characteristics during conversations. Prior metrics for assessing entrainment have focused primarily on surface-level traits; however, prior research has demonstrated that supervised methods can capture more nuanced, lower-level features essential for achieving more precise entrainment measurements. In this work, we examine whether a supervised method developed by Ng and Zellers (2019) can effectively capture entrainment in the form of pitch range convergence. Our findings reveal that the supervised method is indeed sensitive to pitch range entrainment but also introduce limitations when applied to other features. Notably, we observe that the supervised method is prone to capturing loudness entrainment only when certain background conditions are met. Building on this insight, we propose an unsupervised entrainment distance for loudness based on a deep neural network that naturally produces a robust low-dimensional embedding containing loudness information. Our proposed method is applied to the SemEval-2020 Task 6 dataset and demonstrates the ability to model loudness entrainment in a range of acoustic characteristics.

We've developed an open-source suite of web visualization tools tailored for
analyzing spectral and imaging data, which are being utilized in the second edition
of the RCSED galaxy color map. Leveraging web technologies, these browser-based
tools enhance user experience and ease data interpretation. Compared to traditional
software, our web solutions offer greater flexibility as they require no installation
and are accessible across various operating systems and devices. To optimize performance,
we employ lightweight data representation of the galaxy data and advanced caching
techniques. We've chosen public platforms, such as GitHub for coding, and
Zenodo for data hosting, to facilitate collaborative development and data sharing.
Furthermore, our web tools are designed using modular HTML-CSV structure for
portability, allowing users to access source code and data without third-party
interference.

Temporal Action Segmentation, a crucial task in video analysis, involves
identifying distinct actions within a continuous video stream. While current
approaches excel in scenarios with substantial video data, their results suffer
significantly in settings with limited video information. To address this issue,
we propose the Self-supervised Co-occurrence Action Parsing (SSCAP) method,
which tackles the challenge of unsupervised Temporal Action Segmentation in
scenarios with limited video data. SSCAP iteratively refines its understanding
of action sequences through contextual information and local video connections,
ultimately aligning video data with semantic action labels. We also introduce
the Kinetics Charades Gesture (KCG) dataset, a comprehensive, real-world
benchmark for unsupervised Temporal Action Segmentation that incorporates a
wide range of actions, including complex gestures and motion patterns.

We explore the existence of seven hadronic molecular states consisting of $\bar D^{(*)} \Sigma_c^{(*)}$, create associated interpolating currents, and compute their masses, decay constants, and production rates through QCD sum rules. Utilizing current algebra, we then determine their relative production ratios in $\Lambda_b^0$ decays. The study also examines their decay properties and applies the Fierz rearrangement to analyze their ratios in the $J/\psi p$ mass spectrum. The findings suggest the potential observation in future experiments of $\bar D^{*} \Sigma_c^{*}$ molecular states with specific quantum numbers.

Current educational methods promote hands-on learning in software testing, yet many students struggle to apply theoretical principles to practical problems, leading to ineffective test case design. In response, instructors provide extensive feedback to guide students, but this approach can stifle student autonomy and lead to reliance on external guidance. To address this issue, we investigate the benefits of providing feedback that encourages students to discover and learn from their mistakes independently. By adopting inquiry-based learning, students receive conceptual feedback that focuses on the underlying design process rather than individual mistakes, aiming to shift their focus from procedure execution to deeper understanding and improvement. To evaluate the effectiveness of this approach, we conducted a quantitative study comparing student performance in an introductory software engineering course with a traditional multiple-choice question format and a new inquiry-based learning approach that integrates conceptual feedback. Our results indicate that students who received procedural feedback struggled to apply general concepts to subsequent exercises, whereas those provided with conceptual feedback demonstrated improved understanding and could generalize the learned principles to new tasks, leading to increased satisfaction and confidence in their ability to design effective test cases.

Domain adaptation has been applied extensively to handle distribution shifts across various fields. The subcategory, source-free domain adaptation, stands out with its defenseless source model and inaccessible source data. The lack of access to the source data makes domain alignment impossible, and a new paradigm is needed. This work reimagines domain adaptation as a generalization problem after training a network without utilizing source data. A semi-supervised approach is employed to acquire source information via network queries. The source domain's internal structure is assumed to be known, and a new objective, Hypothesis Transfer, is designed to adapt the network based on this information. The Hypothesis Transfer objective is versatile and can be used in various scenarios, such as when the source domain's hypothesis is not precisely known. An additional entropy minimization objective is proposed to improve generalization when the source domain's information is uncertain. The entropy minimization objective is beneficial in three ways: it reduces the network's uncertainty, improves adaptation; and, when combined with Hypothesis Transfer, it enhances generalization. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method on SimCLR, NLP-DVA, VL-DVA, and UDAL benchmarks, surpassing current state-of-the-art methods in cross-database domain adaptation.

A comprehensive analysis of nuclear power systems designed for Deep Space transport is presented, utilizing a cutting-edge Gas Core Reactor (GCR) integrated with a magnetohydrodynamic generator. By overcoming traditional heat transfer obstacles, our innovative heat transfer technology effectively transfers heat to electricity. A detailed examination of the technological advancements required to establish GCR systems is provided, along with an in-depth look at systems configuration, heat transfer efficiency, and performance. Our research reveals that GCR systems are well-suited for Deep Space missions due to their compactness, high efficiency, and ability to generate electricity close to the point of energy consumption. Simulation results demonstrate a specific GCR design capable of generating 100 MW electricity, powered by a compact core measuring just 1 meter in diameter and weighing approximately 500 kg, with an energy conversion efficiency of 30% at 10 kW/g. To achieve this, our technology facilitates heat transfer with an efficiency exceeding 90%, enabling a GCR design that outperforms conventional designs by a factor of three. A detailed examination of the technological and scientific complexities involved in establishing GCR systems is presented, along with an assessment of the scientific and technical readiness of the underlying technologies.

This study presents a novel neural network architecture for particle physics research that leverages localisation information, weight pruning, and reduced data storage. A novel neural network was designed by utilising domain-specific knowledge to pinpoint location interactions within astroparticle detector systems. A localisation sub-network was introduced to bypass traditional topological identifier usage. Weight pruning was implemented to decrease data storage needs during experimental data collection. Utilising domain-specific knowledge, the input data volume was significantly reduced. The proposed sub-network demonstrated a maximum signal enhancement of 6.15 times greater than traditional methods, with a reduction in data storage needs exceeding 50%. The study's findings are expected to contribute to the development of novel domain-specific algorithms for astroparticle particle detection and weight-efficient neural network architecture design.

The development of models for celestial bodies such as brown dwarfs and exoplanets is improved with more accurate representations of their atmospheric properties, including the consideration of molecular absorption. However, this necessitates a substantial increase in data processing complexity. In response, we have created a database, called EXOPLINES, which catalogues the most relevant molecular absorption cross sections within a temperature range of 1000-3000 K that is applicable to the atmospheres of giant exoplanets and brown dwarfs. The data compiled within this database reflect a variety of isotopic compositions and are particularly suitable for applications such as HST and JWST observations. The EXOPLINES database is accessible online at http://exoplines.astro-rit.com.

Answer Set Programming utilizes logic programs to address complex issues, and its effectiveness largely depends on the semantics of models derived from these programs. This semantics is established through an operation called grounding, which converts the logical expressions into a form understandable by solvers. Since grounding is critical, it is essential to have clear, universally applicable guidelines for it. This work provides a foundational framework for grounding, centered around a general format for semantics and a measure of model efficiency. We also introduce specific guidelines for systems implementing Answer Set Programming and discuss how existing systems can adhere to these standards. Furthermore, we explore the challenges associated with parallel processing and XSB logic, proposing concrete methods for handling these complexities.

We have extended quantum resource theories to encompass complex scenarios with multiple intertwined resources that dictate the behavior of physical systems. By formulating a general approach, we have investigated the fundamental principle that links the consumption and production of resources, which we found to be a quantum version of the first law based on conservation of energy. Our framework enables the calculation of a system's residual resource after an arbitrary transformation, which we have effectively mapped onto a tensor calculation. Moreover, we have explored the open quantum quantum resource theories and found that they can be represented on a convex cone, which generalizes the principle of minimum waste, often referred to as Janus head. Our work lays the groundwork for a comprehensive understanding of complex multi-resource scenarios.

We offer a class of estimators for cyber security risk and attack likelihood,
derived from a subfamily of non-linear divergence metrics. Our approach
consists of a series of linear estimators for security metrics characterized
by low statistical complexity, which enables efficient estimation.
We illustrate this method with concrete examples of metric selection,
focusing on differentiated attack strategies and non-differentiated assault vectors.
Our proposed estimator class is validated through empirical analysis of
dataset from the 2020-2022 Capture the Flag events.

We analyze a four-step process for inferring a statistical model of
multivariate time-series data that features varying means, common scaling,
dependence, and heavy-tailed noise across different time points, encompassing
significant shifts in non-stationary patterns. In each step, we utilize a
statistically significant test to evaluate model modifications, starting with
detecting and identifying common scaling patterns, followed by checking for
dependence in individual heavy-tailed noise components, and finally,
investigating non-stationary trends and their interactions. We provide
practical guidelines for implementing these analyses on real-time data and
illustrate the process through two case studies. We also discuss the
underpinnings of each step, highlighting the theoretical foundations,
overviews of relevant methods, and discussing potential alternatives. The
paper's findings are part of a broader research effort to develop a
statistically sound approach for modeling complex data patterns.

A novel set of quantum low-density parity-check codes, denoted qLDC($\delta$,$\rho$,$\alpha$,$\beta$), has been introduced, featuring explicit construction and a probability of error ($<\epsilon$) with decoders processing samples within ($L$) bits per sample, where ($L$) scales as ($\epsilon^{-\alpha}$). We present two specific code families, each tailored to distinct scenarios: qLDC($\delta$,$\rho$,$\alpha$,1/2) for general $\epsilon$, and qLDC($\delta$,$\rho$,3/4,1/2) for smaller $\epsilon$. Both codes possess a probability of error governed by the density evolution, and exhibit a probability of error decreasing exponentially with code size for small $\epsilon$.

The concept of distance-r dominating set was proposed in 2002 for evaluating graph quality. A set of vertices that includes a central hub to cover all vertices within a specific radius r is considered a distance-r dominating set. In this study, the challenge of finding a distance-r dominating set in large, sparse graphs with limited connectivity is addressed. A polynomial-time solution is developed for graphs with tight connections, and another variant is introduced for more general cases, both of which achieve better performance than existing methods on specific graph types.

This research examines the impact of disorder on the correlation between bulk and boundaries in two types of topological insulators, specifically those with an order higher than two. We investigate a two-dimensional topological insulator with bulk topological properties of order three, which can be visualized as a spinless tight-binding model with specific next-to-nearest hopping interactions. Upon introducing random disorder to this model, our findings reveal that bulk topological properties remain intact up to a specific critical disorder threshold. We also identify a diverse array of boundary states, which emerge in response to disorder, depending on its orientation. Similar research was conducted on a three-dimensional topological insulator with bulk topological properties of order three, which can be visualized as a spinless tight-binding model with next-to-nearest hopping interactions in the $k_z$ direction. Upon introducing random $z$-axis disorder, our findings reveal that bulk topological properties remain intact up to a specific critical disorder threshold. We also observe a transition from isolated zero-energy states at the boundary of this topological insulator to a collective zero-energy state appearing at multiple sites on the boundary of three-dimensional topological insulator, which is attributed to disorder-induced correlations between boundary sites.

Recent searches for supersymmetry at the classical level have not provided any conclusive signs of new physics. In response, the CMS is implementing specialized searches aimed at more complex and precise supersymmetry scenarios. This contribution will focus on three new searches using 13 TeV proton-proton collision data recorded with the CMS detector between 2016 and 2018: a heavy gluino search involving the decay of heavy neutralinos and resulting in boosted Z bosons and undetected energy; a search for supersymmetry compression in final states featuring soft tau particles; and an investigation into compressed, long-lived charginos in hadronic final states displaying vanished particle tracks.

Novel view synthesis with light field rendering traditionally achieves accurate epipolar distortion correction and stereoscopic visibility by capturing a comprehensive 4D array of rays. However, capturing such extensive data with high resolution and from multiple perspectives is extremely costly and time-consuming, making it infeasible for most cases. Our approach, Light Field Neural Rendering, addresses this limitation by only capturing a minimal set of 2D images and leveraging a learned, complex light field rendering model to produce the 4D ray data. Our light field simulation model uses an encoder to map scene geometry and a renderer to compute the 4D ray data, which is then optimized using a differentiable loss function. Our experiments show that our approach can produce high-quality light field reconstruction from as few as 12 sparse views with reduced hardware costs compared to traditional methods.

Observations conducted at the SOAR telescope in 2020 along with previously unpublished data, yielded a substantial dataset of 1735 measurements across 1284 targets. Notably, this includes 1273 measurements of 1035 stellar objects, 278 measurements of 217 pairs, 134 single targets, and 10 groups of multiple stars. Among the notable findings, 17 new resolutions were identified, and a maximum resolution of 44 mas was achieved. Moreover, 120 systems with resolved members were able to have their orbital fractions determined.

We will investigate chiral celestial algebras, a type of algebra studied by Baker, Gunaydin and Massa, with an emphasis on their relation to colour-kinematics duality. We find that the chiral algebras of $W_{1+\infty}$, the chiral oscillator algebra and the higher $W_{1+\infty}$ family, all have a structure that can be described as spacetime-multiplying, a concept developed by us. This means we will build four self-dual self-dual dual theories, one for each type of algebra, using the bulk duals of self-dual theories. We will also show that these theories are in line with the chiral aspects of the four-point functions of the theories based on the chiral $M_{2n+3}$ algebra. We will use the chiral aspects of the four-point functions of the theories based on the $W_{1+\infty}$ algebra to show that the aspects of the four-point functions of the Baker-Gunaydin-Massa algebra have an analytic continuation to the aspects of the four-point functions of the theories based on the $M_{2n+3}$ algebra. We will also show that the aspects of the four-point functions of the theories based on the $W_{1+\infty}$ algebra have an analytic continuation to the aspects of the four-point functions of the theories based on the $M_{2n+3}$ algebra. A powerful shock wave resulting from a major solar flare or coronal mass ejection can significantly impact the surrounding area by transferring energy and momentum. This phenomenon was recently detected using LOFAR's wide-field capabilities, as the shock wave produced by a highly inclined jet interacting with the solar corona's surface. The observed shock wave had an estimated speed of 130 km/s, which surpassed the jet's initial velocity. As a result, the piston shock persisted for only a short period of 1.5 minutes before disappearing from LOFAR's data. The transmitted pressure through the coronal interface caused the piston shock to weaken and eventually disappear.

A detailed likelihood analysis is performed on the general two Higgs doublet model in light of observed anomalies in rare decays of $B$ mesons, as well as the $W$ boson decay and muon's anomalous magnetic moment. The model's parameters are investigated through a comprehensive study at 68 and 90% confidence levels. The results indicate that the model is consistent with experimental data, particularly in its ability to account for observed anomalies and the $W$ boson decay. The findings also suggest that the muon's anomalous magnetic moment offers the strongest constraint on the model's parameters. The study's outcomes are further validated by a corresponding correlation analysis.

This study introduces a novel, simplified mathematical model for the random movement of vortices in two-dimensional turbulent flows. These types of flows are prevalent in numerous applications, including atmospheric and ocean currents. The model built upon prior research by Chorin, which applied a stochastic differential equation to capture the finite-time fractal behavior of these vortices. Our contribution consists of two key aspects: Firstly, we have converted the original equation into a more complex stochastic process with higher order parameters, which facilitates numerical calculations. Secondly, we have formulated a functional differential equation to represent the long-term behavior of these vortices as a function of their position and velocity history. Our numerical simulations demonstrate both the short-range and long-term behaviors of these vortices.

The state vector of a boson sampling process can be precisely generating functionally represented using a specific sequence of parameters, which are determined by invariant polynomials in the Schrodinger picture. Utilizing these generating functions, the full state vector of any boson sampling configuration or quantum process can be directly computed without needing access to its density matrix. In this study, the analysis is extended to examine two-person entanglement in the boson sampling process. A measure of two-person entanglement is defined and calculated for multiple boson systems in both general and boson sampling contexts. In the boson sampling context, the two-person entanglement is found to be completely described by a single real number value. A comprehensive set of boson sampling configurations is systematically examined to understand how increasing the number of bosons affects entanglement patterns. Key findings include the discovery that two-person entanglement is generally present in boson sampling processes with fewer bosons, but absent in processes with specific numbers of bosons. Entanglement patterns are linked to the underlying Fock space basis and two-person correlation functions.

Temporal sequence analysis typically employs spectral-based methods like Spectral Embeddings to compactly represent sequence data, making it easier for supervised learning algorithms to use. These methods have been particularly useful in the life sciences, where long-standing issues with data dimensionality have limited the effectiveness of many learning methods. However, while Spectral Embeddings address data dimensionality, they can introduce a separate issue of lost information in low-dimensional representations. To mitigate this, we propose selecting an optimal spectral embedding for each sample, but this approach is computationally impractical for large datasets. An alternative method involves using a pre-embedding step to reduce temporal sequence data, but this can also introduce information loss. To avoid this, we recommend skipping the pre-embedding step and applying Spectral Embeddings only when necessary, directly feeding the resulting spectral features into a variety of supervised learning algorithms. We demonstrate this approach with the analysis of two widely-used cytometry datasets, showcasing improved performance and cost efficiency.

Reinforcement learning seeks to develop the most effective strategies through interactions with complex systems, even when the underlying rules are unknown. Many successful methods employ high-performance deep neural networks, but the theoretical foundation and corresponding algorithmic implementations often diverge. This research aims to bridge this gap by illustrating that specific neural network architectures can be viewed as iterations of a key update rule from the literature, also utilized in particle filtering algorithms used in statistics. This connection sheds light on the "belief states" used in decision-making through reinforcement learning, especially in partially observable environments. Several popular algorithms can be understood as particular cases of a general approach, also revealing the existence of a specific "infinite network" that is optimal, and can be used to develop novel observation-transformation learning methods.

In video action detection, current research often relies on classifying actions based on spatial and temporal features extracted from 2D or 3D convolutional networks. However, these methods overlook important contextual cues like the objects present in a video, which help define an action. In this work, we tackle the challenge of weakly-supervised action detection by developing a novel model that integrates self-attention and graph convolutional networks to capture contextual information. Our GCN-based model aggregates object information from diverse sources by treating objects as nodes in an graph and learning their weights through self-attention. By doing so, it can inform the action classification model, leading to more accurate action recognition. Our method demonstrates superior performance on ActivityNet, COIN, and Kinetics400 by achieving a significant improvement over existing state-of-the-art models on multiple benchmarks.

A recent competition, the 2021 Image Similarity Challenge, introduced a benchmark dataset to evaluate state-of-the-art image copy detection methods. With a total of 123 participants involved, the winning entries are analyzed and compared in this report. The top performers are highlighted, revealing effective approaches to detecting copied images, such as utilizing advanced neural networks and combining multiple detection techniques. Moreover, the study explores the most successful strategy's limitations and identifies common errors, like overemphasizing image surface details. To facilitate future progress in copied image detection, the report provides detailed analysis of each challenge stage and offers recommendations for future research.

This research focuses on the analysis of boundary-value problems for random processes with degenerate diffusion characteristics, stemming from degenerate elliptic equations.  We investigate the asymptotic behavior of a family of boundary-value problems as a small parameter approaches zero, with implications that can manifest as metastability effects.  Our approach encompasses various scenarios, including the homogenization of a model describing the propagation of heat in a family of thin tubes.  Specifically, we examine the behavior of a family of boundary-value problems for Bessel processes in a degenerate environment as a small parameter $\varepsilon$ approaches zero, with associated boundary conditions specified on a set that shrinks as $\varepsilon \rightarrow 0$.  In a related model, we analyze the asymptotic behavior of a family of boundary-value problems for processes in a degenerate environment with associated boundary conditions specified on a set that shrinks towards an irregular point $O$.  In addition, we investigate the asymptotic behavior of a family of boundary-value problems for processes in a degenerate environment with associated boundary conditions specified on a set that approaches a hypersurface of irregularity $S$ towards the point $O$.

This study focuses on the characteristics of nuclear matter at zero temperature within the influence of intense magnetic fields by applying the lowest order constraint variational (LOCV) method, utilizing the $AV_{18}$ nuclear potential. We discovered that the absence of a magnetic field results in an energy per particle symmetric function in relation to the spin polarization parameter. As a result, our calculations indicate that no spontaneous transition to a ferromagnetic state occurs in nuclear matter at the ground state. However, our analysis shows that magnetic fields strengths above 35 million Gauss can drive the system into a ferromagnetic state, contingent on the specific value of the effective mass.

  We established that the effective mass plays a crucial role in determining the preferred spin alignment of the fermions in nuclear matter under the influence of intense magnetic fields, with the lowest possible effective mass corresponding to the strongest fermion alignment. 

  Our analysis of the impact of magnetic fields on the energy per particle, spin polarization parameter, and effective mass revealed a complex relationship, with the former increasing and the latter decreasing in response to an applied magnetic field.

Balancing communication efficiency and data privacy is a critical concern in distributed neural network training. To address this issue, we have created an innovative approach that reconciles the requirements of efficient communication and differential privacy. We integrated Relative Entropy Coding, a highly efficient compression technique, into the distributed training framework. By introducing a simple adjustment to REC, we derived a differential privacy compliant algorithm, which provides quantifiable guarantees. Experimental results show that our approach substantially decreases communication costs while maintaining high data privacy standards.

A comprehensive far-ultraviolet photometric survey of the Taurus-Auriga-Perseus complex has been conducted, using the far-ultraviolet camera GUVI on board the NASA spacecraft TOPEX/Poseidon during its operational period from 1992 to1998. The survey covered an area of approximately 7500 square degrees, with an estimated 98% of the Taurus complex's far-ultraviolet emission being detected. A total of 1357 far-ultraviolet sources with luminosities exceeding 10^31 erg s^-1 were identified, with about 1220 sources located within the Taurus complex itself. A correlation between luminosity and temperature was established for the young stellar objects within the Taurus complex, with near-infrared wavelength photometry confirming the identification of 776 sources from the survey, according to the X-ray to far-ultraviolet luminosity ratio. The density of young stellar objects within the survey's coverage area was estimated to be around 0.7 parsec^-2, with approximately 60% of the young stellar objects within the Taurus complex being identified as classical T Tauri stars. A significant number of Herbig-Haro objects and Herbig-Haro complexes within the survey's coverage area were also mapped, with 75% of the Herbig-Harp complexes within the Taurus complex itself. Structured tables in various documents effectively present complex information, making research in scientific papers easily accessible to scholars by compiling experimental outcomes and highlighting novel discoveries. Current table analysis techniques can struggle with complex PDFs found in diverse datasets, leading to poor extraction results. This research addresses the table extraction challenge by employing Graph Neural Networks and representation embedding techniques to break down the process into two sub-tasks: table detection and cell content extraction. The proposed method is tested on the SciTSR and TabProcesing benchmarks.

This work delves into the dynamic cognitive hierarchy theory, introduced by Sjstrm (1993), within the context of multi-stage incomplete information games. In such scenarios, players simultaneously uncover both game rules and personal type information. Building on his approach, we establish a rigorous definition of a dynamic cognitive hierarchy of different inference abilities. We then examine the three most fundamental decision-making types: Inferior, Equal, and Superior Cognitive Hierarchy Players.  Inferior Cognitive Hierarchy Players assume types are relatively simple, while Equal Hierarchy Players assume types are uniformly distributed.  By contrast, Superior Cognitive Hierarchy Players assume types are uniformly distributed, with their own being distinct. We then explore the three most fundamental decision-making types: Inference, Inference and Observation, and Simultaneous Inference and Observation.  In such scenarios, nature reveals game rules through a sequence of observations, while players simultaneously uncover their type. We then derive best response strategies for each decision-making type and show how these strategies compare to simpler strategies, such as pure type behavior.  In such cases, players either adopt the same strategy regardless of type or adopt different strategies based on type. Precise and continuous population estimates are crucial for policy decisions, particularly in countries with limited censuses. For these areas, indirect estimation methods utilizing remote sensing data and population data patterns are adopted. Nevertheless, the success of these methods in Mozambique is hindered by the absence of recent censuses and the challenges of data alignment. The population growth rate fluctuations in the region also complicate these estimates. This paper investigates the obstacles in estimating the population of Mozambique and presents potential solutions for accurate census-independent estimation. The study combines censuses data, UN population forecasts, and satellite imagery from the Advanced Land Imagination System to analyze census results, UN data, and historical population trends. The results indicate that the center of population in Mozambique has shifted, largely due to rural-to-urban migration. The estimation methods in the country are further complicated by the presence of dense forests that obstruct satellite data. The study finds that the alignment of satellite data with population data patterns is the primary challenge in estimating the population in Mozambique. The results highlight the importance of recent censuses data and the center of population in achieving accurate estimates. The study concludes that the alignment of data from various sources is the primary challenge in estimating the population in Mozambique.

Over the past ten years, substantial advancements have been made in reducing the number of unnecessary hits in data retrieval systems, particularly those based on hash tables. A significant step was taken recently in developing new types of data retrieval systems called approximate query filters. These innovative systems ensure a certain minimum standard of accuracy by guaranteeing a certain rate of correctness, which in turn allows them to function with a minimal number of data elements, referred to as the size of the filter. They achieve this by maintaining a substantially reduced dataset, referred to as the filter, which in turn enables faster search times. A major drawback of current approximate query filters is that they still contribute to a certain percentage of incorrect hits, which in turn results in some data elements being incorrectly removed from the filter, thus affecting its size. A novel approach has been proposed in this study to design a new type of data retrieval system, referred to as a false positive free filter, which aims to minimize data retrieval time by ensuring zero percentage of incorrect hits, which in turn enables it to achieve a faster search rate. A novel data structure, referred to as the free extension of range summary, has been introduced in this study to design a false positive free filter with an optimal size, which in turn enables it to achieve a faster search rate.
