We're investigating multiple correlated electron processes triggered by a photoinduced reaction that creates molecules from coexisting spin-isomer states in a single atomic species. Specifically, we're focusing on a scenario where two atoms in a state of spin polarization that matches can combine with a nearby atom of the same spin orientation to form a triatomic molecule with all three atoms in a state of spin polarization that doesn't match. Our research shows that this type of photoinduced reaction results in the creation of molecule-isomer states in a particular manifold with two less units of spin polarization that are not matched, and that this type of photoinduced reaction results in the creation of molecule-isomer states in a particular manifold with two less units of spin polarization that are not matched, and that this type of photoinduced reaction results in the de-excitation of specific hyperfine states in a particular manifold with six units of spin polarization that are not matched, and that this type of photoinduced reaction results in the creation of molecule-isomer states in a particular manifold with six units of spin polarization that are not matched, and that this type of photoinduced reaction results in the creation of molecule-isomer states in a particular manifold with six units of spin polarization that are not matched, and that this type of photoinduced reaction results in the creation of molecule-isomer states in a particular manifold with six units of spin polarization that are not matched, and that this type of photoinduced reaction results in the creation of molecule

We introduce a novel SPH method that incorporates a multi-resolution approach to tackle multi-phase fluid-structure interaction problems. This method adapts a part of the domain at a coarser resolution to reduce computational complexity, while maintaining high fidelity at the interface between phases. To achieve this, we employ a multi-resolution basis for the continuous pressure field, resulting in a well-posed weak formulation. This is further evaluated using a multi-step time-integration scheme that maintains stability and accuracy. The coarsening strategy is also thoroughly examined, and our results confirm the theoretical analysis. A comparison with the standard SPH method highlights the efficiency gains of the multi-resolution approach. Lastly, we demonstrate its capabilities on two intricate FSI examples, showcasing its potential for accurate and efficient simulation.

Due to the diverse applications of machine learning, its ability to identify patterns in datasets is well-established, albeit limited by the rapid growth of computation time with data size. A shift towards quantum computing could potentially resolve this issue, providing an alternative to current statistical models. We investigate an advanced quantum processor, capable of solving both supervised and unsupervised learning problems, by applying it to datasets from binary and multiclass origins. We demonstrate that the quantum processor can learn and accurately predict outcomes for binary classification problems, while the performance of unsupervised clustering is deemed insufficient when compared to established methods. Additionally, a cross-validation technique is applied to determine the optimal number of qubits required for successful problem-solving.

A recently created TTS model called FastPitch can change pitch, but the quality of the speech made with it gets significantly worse when it's given pitch values far from its average pitch value.  In other words, it can only control pitch so much.  We suggest two new algorithms to fix this issue.  First, we came up with a pitch-shifting technique that doesn't change a speaker's unique voice characteristics, which helps make new speech samples sound more natural.  We also developed a training technique that uses a small collection of speech samples from various pitches instead of just a single pitch.  We call this collection a "pitch wheel."  We tested our algorithms and found that they let FastPitch control pitch more easily and make higher-quality speech samples.  Our model can even be used with smaller collections of speech samples, which makes it easier to change the pitch.

This research focuses on developing spatiotemporal reasoning models that learn from videos like humans, leveraging a large dataset with complex temporal relationships and spatial context. We introduce Hopper, a cutting-edge multi-hop model that sequentially generates a concept tree to infer temporal relationships between objects, and demonstrates superior performance on a prominent visual reasoning benchmark, outperforming state-of-the-art models with enhanced efficiency. For in-depth exploration, the code is publicly available on our GitHub repository, and the model's parameters can be fine-tuned on Google Cloud AI Platform.

Our study investigates lepton-pair production coupled with bottom quarks at the Large Hadron Collider using theoretical predictions from next-to-leading order QCD. The investigation encompasses various factors, including a detailed analysis of predicted outcomes and an estimation of the associated uncertainties based on the dependence on perturbative QCD parameters. Additionally, it involves a comparative evaluation of parton-shower models and matching schemes to propose an improved procedure that includes the effects of bottom quarks on neutral-current Drell-Yan production beyond tree-level complexity. Specifically, we examine pairs of identical leptons (same-flavor, opposite-sign) associated with bottom quarks in separate experimental windows defined by lepton-pair invariant mass (below 66 GeV, between 66-88 GeV, between 88-94 GeV, and above 94 GeV) to minimize interference from other background processes. Based on a simulated dataset of 139 fb$^{-1}$, it is determined that the same-flavor, opposite-sign lepton-pair production with an invariant mass above 66 GeV can contribute approximately 1.1 pb to the total production cross-section, resulting in a measurable $W$ mass with an accuracy of 100 MeV, provided that the top quark mass is known with a precision of 500 MeV.

To effectively use telepresence robots (TRSs), it's crucial to ensure a positive user experience despite potential network disruptions. Loss of network control over TRSs can be particularly stressful and clear quality of experience guidelines are missing. Researchers achieved significant reductions in perceived delay and loss rates for TRS videos by employing interactive video quality assessment. They used the VQM metric in a live TRS stream to estimate QoE and implemented this measure as an alarm system to trigger robottical actions when quality falls below a set threshold. A low-cost remote control was used to enable swift manual control of the TRS when network disruptions occur. Evaluations with human subjects showed that interactive VQM provides an effective QoE management approach for remote controlling TRSs.

In this study, three Bayesian hierarchical regression models were fitted to the data of Tenerife bulging process to forecast future performance, with the aim of investing in the market with optimal portfolio strategies. The first model integrated prior knowledge into its structure, the second incorporated additional market insights into the mean, and the third combined both scenarios. Among the three models, the one that combined prior knowledge and mean optimization performed best, with the within-group model comparisons indicating that Tenerife's returns correlated with those of the market, and our analysis revealed significant excess volatility. A subsequent investigation of the model's components showed that the prior knowledge model accurately estimated Tenerife's mean return, indicating that its returns were normally distributed with a low mean, negative variance, and moderately negative correlation.

The game "Mafia," also known as "Werewolf," is a party-based competition between two opposing groups. Citizens and mafia members are the main groups. Each phase in the game, consisting of day and night segments, allows for different actions to occur. During the day, citizens can vote to eliminate suspected mafia members, with the goal of eradicating the mafia through majority voting. At night, the mafia can attack citizens, with the possibility of potentially killing them. This work develops a model to calculate the long-term ratio of dead to living players, denoted as $r_{d}$, in the game's initial stages. The model takes into account the number of mafia members, their actions, and whether or not they are discovered by the citizens. The model also considers different possible night actions for the mafia. Finally, we explore some potential applications and limitations of the model.

Several planetary systems have multiple giant planets, and research aims to
understand how their formation is affected when planets develop in tandem. Our
study employs long-term computer simulations of planetary growth from a shared
disk, and the results reveal a link between the planets' relative sizes and the
formation of gaps in the disk. However, when both planets grow simultaneously,
their masses converge to a narrow range over a relatively short period of time.
Delaying one planet's growth causes it to catch up with the other's mass growth
after a brief lag. Ultimately, the key factor determining a planet's final
mass in our simulations is the depth of indentations created by the other planet in
the disk, and this influences gas accretion rates.

The electrical conductivity of an ensemble of nanomaterials on a macroscopic scale
depends on intricate electronic transport mechanisms, which involve the combined effect
of strong interplay between electronic currents and vibrational waves. To study this
phenomenon, the dynamic properties of single-walled carbon nanotubes were examined in
relation to their thermal motion. An armchair nanotube film served as the subject of
this investigation, providing a system in which to analyze transverse electron vibrations.
Using an innovative technique to measure electron properties, the interplay between
vibrational waves and electronic currents was identified through analysis of
electrical conductivity while subjected to various temperatures. Computational models
based on microscopic processes revealed that intra-nanotube and inter-nanotube electronic
processes occur simultaneously and are influenced by temperature. Notably, the
computational results indicate that inter-nanotube electronic currents are primarily
driven by inter-nanotube vibrational waves, while the vibrational waves within
individual nanotubes facilitate intra-nanotube electronic currents. These findings
emphasize the significance of considering combined vibrational waves of individual
nanomaterials in understanding macroscopic electrical conductivity of nanomaterials.

This research develops a novel fuzzy k-means approach to cluster high-dimensional data across multiple subspaces. The algorithm is specifically designed to identify tight and separated clusters. Its core component is a variable feature weight calculation method based on entropy, which ensures that features with the most cluster-separating information have the highest weights. The proposed approach also incorporates a local optimisation step to improve the entropy measure and thus the overall performance. Additionally, our analysis proves the local optimality and uniqueness of the algorithm under certain conditions. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated through multiple datasets and comparisons with common clustering algorithms.

Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have become crucial components of various neural networks and ensemble learning systems. Nevertheless, traditional algorithms designed for learning MoE models often struggle to converge due to getting stuck in local optima, a challenge that persists despite extensive research over two decades. In an effort to address this issue, we introduce a novel approach, consisting of a dynamic gate optimization method and a new clustering technique that incorporates a unique distance metric. This new method boasts theoretical guarantees for learning MoE clusters and is remarkably more efficient than existing approaches, achieving a significant reduction in computational time and strong performance on a range of synthetic and real-world data sets.

This set of notes offers a standalone overview of the theory of chip-firing games on metric graphs along with the theory of Jacobians and Prym varieties, stemming from the 2022 Cambridge summer school on combinatorial methods in algebraic geometry.

While quantum gravitational effects generally break global symmetries, their impact on light propagation in vacuum remains unknown. This study explores the possibility of quantum gravitational birefringence arising from globally symmetric fields undergoing quantum breakdown during quantum gravitational effects, such as the Casimir effect. We demonstrate that the birefringence induced by this process could be detectable through observations of the polarization of the cosmic microwave background. Notably, its magnitude would be comparable to that of the axion effect at a much weaker gravitational field intensity, specifically $H\sim 10^{-19}$ GeV$^{-1}$. This finding implies that quantum gravitational effects representing diverse mechanisms could collectively yield substantial birefringence, a phenomenon potentially within the capacity of forthcoming observational data to detect.

Our research presents new findings on the UV-bright stars within the globular cluster NGC 4147, obtained through the UVIT instrument on AstroSat. The investigation involved 11 bright stars in the ultraviolet (UV) region, rather than the visible region, to explore their nature. The diversity among these stars allows for the possibility that some may be blue horizontal branch (BHB) stars, while others could be field stars within the Milky Way or objects other than a BHB. To accurately classify these stars as a BHB, we employed various statistical and photometric methods, but an unambiguous decision cannot be made at this time. Further observations in the visible region using the EMCCD and SCA detectors on board AstroSat are necessary to reach a conclusive finding.

This note presents a new category of map functions known as oriented colored broken submersions, which forms the most basic type of map functions that adhere to the b-principle, and is nearly equivalent to the set of oriented submersions in 2 dimensions. It demonstrates that the Madsen-Weiss theorem, which can be viewed as a variation of the standard Mumford Conjecture, is derivable from a specific application of the b-principle to oriented colored broken submersions, combined with the findings from Harer's stability theorem and Miller and Morita's work.

Recent research in deep learning has identified two widely accepted principles: 
1) Transferable tasks share similar data distributions, and
2) Large variations in label data can hinder a model's ability to generalize.
These findings underpin fundamental principles in supervised learning, yet they are contradicted by the remarkable performance of computer vision models, which often achieve high generalization performance despite diverse label data and non-typical datasets.
This paradox suggests that the concepts of data distribution and label uniformity may not be essential for understanding generalization in deep learning models.
This paper challenges the two consensus by demonstrating that transferability and generalization are influenced by factors outside of data distribution and label uniformity, such as the specific task itself.

In various scenarios, such as mobilization, disease spread, and rumor dissemination, the understanding of information diffusion processes across networks is crucial. Real-world applications often demand the rapid dissemination of information. However, certain situations, like preventing the spread of diseases or preventing the spread of misinformation, require slower diffusion rates. We propose a model where the temporal evolution of a diffusion process is influenced by the average degree of connectivity and the community structure of a growing network. Our analytical model reveals that the speed of information diffusion is directly tied to the network's modularity, degree exponent, and growth rate. Our findings are further validated through numerical simulations, showcasing the diverse effects of modularity on diffusion speed. Ultimately, by controlling a network's growth strategy, the system can be designed to either accelerate or slow down the information diffusion process.

Under specific conditions from Floer theory, we derive numerical measures indicating the proximity of two Lagrangians based on their angular separation, and these measurements depend on how close those Lagrangian angles are to being perfectly aligned. Some outcomes resulting from these conditions are a definitive uniqueness proof for special Lagrangians and a detailed criterion describing the process by which a collection of varifolds converges towards a special Lagrangian, with this criterion itself dependent on Lagrangian angles.

The reliability of a discrete-time channel model that uses a standard method of perturbation
is numerically investigated for cases without signal amplification. We assess the distance between 
discrete nonlinear interference points and find that this distance can be employed to estimate 
the effective memory length of the channel.

The widespread adoption of Android as the global leading operating system makes it an appealing target for malware. To counter this threat, security experts continuously develop advanced detection systems based on machine learning. However, the success of these systems has inadvertently encouraged malicious actors to adapt and evolve as a response. This growth in Android malware has shifted from basic evasion tactics to more sophisticated forms of evasion, aimed at deceiving detection systems. This research aims to explore evasion attacks on Android OS, with a focus on exploring the various types of evasion, their prevalence, and their impact on Android malware, as well as the ways Android detection systems have been affected by evasion attacks. By examining the different types of evasion, this research seeks to highlight the need for a unified approach to evasion research and detection.

Service-oriented computing utilizes services, which are self-contained applications, to construct large systems. When numerous services interact, complexities arise, particularly in managing the services' execution sequences. To address these challenges, the concept of workflow has been introduced, referring to the coordinated execution of services. As the number of services increased, managing them became difficult, leading to the development of the idea of generic workflows, which can incorporate various services. In this study, we introduce Ozy, a orchestration container that can be used across different hosting environments, while other systems, such as WS-BPEL and XProc, are specific protocol implementations. Our goals are to analyze existing orchestration methods, identify common problems, and design a general, adaptable solution. By defining a standard abstract structure for workflows, which can be hostedly interpreted, we aim to enable seamless support for multiple services. Our proposed Ozy container structure is based on this understanding. To demonstrate its usability, we show how Ozy can be employed with existing services, such as WS-BEL, to define workflows. Our analysis indicates that Ozy can efficiently manage common problems, such as service variability and data handling.

Recent experimental observations supporting the paucity of non-chiral, topological states have led to a widely accepted understanding that complex intermingling of Landau levels eliminates all topological states except for standard fractional quantum Hall states.  This conclusion, however, is based on a simplified model where energy mixing increases gradually.  In reality, moderate increases in moderate Landau-level mixing lead to novel states that are absent in the one-dimensional model.  A comprehensive study of the complete phase diagram of 5/2 state is presented, including gapped, gapless, and halving phases, as well as non-chiral, chiral, Kramers-pairing topological phases, with moderate Landau-level mixing strength increasing.  The study shows that there are five distinct phases: gapped, gapless, halving, chiral, and non-chiral topological phases.  The study also shows that moderate Landau-level mixing leads to an unusual reentrant gapped phase that is absent in one-dimensional models.

Our analysis reveals that the conditions generating the Thakurta metric, previously investigated in a study by Böhm et al., involve a single star undergoing a rapid collapse without any preceding main sequence evolution, however, this is contradicted by prior research suggesting single star collapses do not yield the Thakurta metric. Furthermore, even if a rapid collapse occurred, this would not result in a global mean density high enough to dominate the early universe. Consequently, the possibility of the Thakurta metric describing primordial black holes seems unlikely. If this is the case, then the bounds on primordial black holes proposed by the LIGO-Virgo collaboration would remain unchanged.

The complexity of factors influencing gas giant and mini-Neptune formation through pebble accretement is acknowledged, with our research focusing on the impact of ambient density perturbations. We've discovered that within a 100 km radius of a forming planet, perturbations triggered by the planet itself or other nearby objects can either hinder or facilitate pebble growth on solid cores. This results from the perturbations either increasing or decreasing the area where pebbles can accumulate, affecting the core's growth. Employing a simplified model, we've mapped out the formation pathways of solid cores in response to varying levels of ambient density perturbations, with our findings suggesting that the formation of massive planets on external protoplanetary disk structures and low-mass cores on high-mass cores are two feasible scenarios.

Extremely large, overparameterized models have achieved impressive success. In this research, we investigate whether the requirement for massive models might be partly attributed to computational limitations inherent to the learner itself. We also examine whether these constraints are exacerbated under robust learning conditions. Our study indicates that this is indeed the case. Specifically, we demonstrate that a simple binary classification problem necessitates an enormous model size if we are to approximate the performance of a robust optimizer like the $\ell_2$-projected gradient descent method. Moreover, we establish that a specific form of computational limitation, characterized by a fixed number of operations per step, imposes a minimum model size that grows with the problem input $d$. Our results also reveal that a particular form of computational constraint inherent to fixed-point iteration leads to a comparable, albeit milder, lower bound. We also provide a complementary result, showing that a specific form of decay in the learning rate can yield a model size that grows logarithmically with $d$.

Three results concerning the presence of Bohr sets in sumsets within countable discrete abelian groups are demonstrated. Significant to number theory, Bohr sets can be thought of as a modified version of the p-adic numbers. These results expand upon a previously established outcome by Bergelson and Host, which only showed the existence of Bohr sets in sumsets within the integers, unless a specific measure is zero. Additionally, one of the proven outcomes aligns with a prior theorem by Bergelson, Furstenberg, and Host, which also applies to the integers. Lastly, another outcome is a generalization of a recently discovered result by the researcher.

This study addresses the dial-a-ride problem within large urban settings, where we've limited demand for shared transportation. We've developed a mixed-integer linear programming model that accounts for customer convenience during vehicle routing, and CUT has emerged as a crucial branch-and-cut method to prevent solvability. Through initial evaluations, it became apparent that Cut has a non-trivial tendency to create empty branches. To rectify this issue, two supplementary cut techniques, derived from the theory of polynomial h-convergence, have been introduced to enhance branch-and-cut performance. Numerical experiments have demonstrated the efficacy of these cuts in cutting branch times and identifying feasible solutions.

This study explores multi-modal pretraining techniques for product data in E-commerce, addressing limitations in current methods which struggle with modality-noise and modality-missing. We introduce K3M, a novel method incorporating knowledge modality to mitigate noise and supplement missing modalities in image and text data. K3M utilizes a modality-specific feature extraction module, a modality-agnostic pretraining module, and a modality-agnostic projection module to process the three modalities simultaneously. The proposed method allows End-to-end K3M to handle any combination of image, text, and knowledge data, as well as missing modalities, while standardizing the feature representation for visible modalities through pretraining. Experiments on E-commerce product datasets demonstrate K3M's superior performance compared to existing multi-modal models.

A significant challenge in Alzheimer's research involves determining an individual's likelihood of progressing to the disease, given their current cognitive state. To tackle this issue, our team employed the Deep InfoMax method, combining it with a contrastive learning framework, to train a neural network that generates comprehensive cognitive profiles from available data. By maximizing the mutual information between the network's forward and inverse operations, we ensured that the profiles accurately represent an individual's current cognitive status, and that the profiles generated by the network are unique to each subject. Additionally, our approach ensures that the profiles are consistent across different subjects. Experimental results demonstrate that our trained network produces high-quality profiles that effectively distinguish between subjects who have progressed to Alzheimer's disease and those who have not.

Natural Language Processing employs a crucial task called text classification, which sequential models efficiently handle, though their connection to linguistic semantics in output predictions often falls short. This study presents an innovative score called I-score, an innovative operator called interaction operator $inter$, and an innovative model called Interaction-based Recurrent Neural Networks (IRNN) that effectively incorporates linguistic semantics for text classification. The interaction operator allows for merging sub-strings' features into a comprehensive feature, which can then be used in text classification. When applied to IRNN, the I-score exhibits superior performance with significant improvements in various datasets, thus surpassing leading recurrent models, including LSTM and GRU.

We examine how external magnetic fields influence spin-orbit coupling in systems with strong correlations, such as those found in half-metals and Weyl semmetals, where spin and charge are coupled. When these materials are placed in a magnetic environment, a phenomenon known as magnon-induced spin-orbit coupling arises, which causes spins to become mixed due to the interaction with magnetic excitations, resulting in lattices with spin properties. This effect can lead to the suppression of spin transport and the suppression of topological properties in these materials. Key differences emerge between systems with high and low levels of spin polarization, as well as between different types of orbital symmetries. This research opens up new avenues for controlling spin properties in complex magnetic materials.

We've developed an alternative approach to light Dark Matter, grounded in the principle of metastability. This new path offers a quantifiable link between Dark Matter density and the cosmological constant observed in our universe. Our proposal comprises two parts: Metastable Dark Matter, where Dark Matter particles are initially unstable and decay into stable particles at the universe's inception, with some still lingering today; and Metastable Dark Matter Conformal, where Dark Matter particles experience a confining phase transition at a scale planckian to the confining scale. This confining phase transition is linked to the formation of the cosmological constant. This theory can be tested through future observations of Dark Matter lifetimes and the cosmological constant's evolution over time.

To ensure that AI-powered medical devices operate correctly in diverse environments, it's crucial to evaluate their performance accurately even when encountering new, unforeseen scenarios. Conformal prediction offers a promising approach to addressing this challenge by providing reliable predictions in various settings. In this study, we apply a variant of conformal prediction known as i.i.d. conformal prediction to compare the effectiveness of traditional hypothesis testing in validating medical devices against the conformal prediction framework. Our analysis focuses on estimating the conditional coverage probability of a predictive model with no assumed underlying model. Through a simulation-based study, we examine the convergence of conformal prediction's conditional coverage probability to the true value under different scenarios. Additionally, we investigate the convergence rate of conformal prediction's estimator of the empirical error rate. Our findings suggest that conformal prediction outperforms traditional testing, especially in complex scenarios.

High-fidelity simulations of DNA's atomic structure have become more feasible with advanced computational capabilities. Nonetheless, standard atomistic simulations fall short of capturing the complete picture of DNA's functional and structural properties. This limitation arises from the slow timescales governing large conformational changes and the sampling of DNA's less favored states. To overcome this challenge, our research introduces novel molecular dynamics tools for modeling rigid segments of DNA. These tools, drawn from existing methods, can significantly enhance sampling and facilitate the exploration of DNA's less constrained states. When applied to a 50K base pair simulation of double-stranded DNA, our results demonstrate a 3000-fold boost in transitions between sub-angstrom conformational states. To validate these results, our findings align with experimental and theoretical data on DNA's flexibility. Importantly, our research also highlights the value of theoretical representations of DNA's flexible components in capturing its mechanical properties. Furthermore, our results show a substantial increase (two orders of magnitude) in exploring transition barriers between large conformational states. Overall, our research demonstrates the effectiveness of theoretical representations of DNA's components in simulations and opens up new avenues for the study of DNA's functions and structures through enhanced sampling techniques.

The Advanced Narrow-Screen entropy encoding developed by Ford & Moore (2011) claims a superior gain in efficiency over the widely used Huffman encoding. We compared the performance of ANS and Huffman encoding on a dataset of Narrow-Screen images, and found that both encodings have comparable efficiency. Additionally, since they use the same entropy encoding methods, there is little motivation to use ANS instead of Huffman encoding. The use of ANS in the lossless image compression tool ZPAQ has not resulted in significant file size reduction. The main advantage of ANS encoding is its ability to perform progressive decoding, which may be beneficial in specific applications. However, since ZPAQ already offers progressive decoding capabilities, there is no additional benefit from using ANS encoding.

The dielectric characteristics of micro- and mesoporous materials are heavily influenced by the composition and presence of liquid phases. Electrolyte dielectric behavior is influenced by the balance between its ionic and bulk water components. Our study focuses on the dielectric properties of cement-based material pore solutions using advanced numerical methods, incorporating both cement paste and aggregate paste's pore solution models. These models were developed based on experimental data through nuclear magnetic resonance and were validated against dielectric measurements at various frequencies and temperatures. Our results reveal that cement paste's pore solution exhibits dielectric behavior similar to that of a 0.2 M NaCl solution at elevated concentrations, but transitions to a Debye-like behavior upon drying. In contrast, aggregate paste exhibits dielectric behavior akin to 6 M NaCl. Our findings can be applied to assess the service life of reinforced cement structures by using dielectric methods to evaluate chloride content and early-stage hydration progression.

In our earlier work, the range of heavy-antiheavy hadronic molecules was mapped out. This time, we're exploring the landscape of heavy-heavy hadronic molecules, taking into account experimental observations and theoretical predictions to highlight notable examples. It's evident that heavy-heavy hadronic molecules offer a unique window into the quark-gluon structure of these particles, complex entities composed of multiple constituent parts that raise questions regarding their existence as genuine particles. As such, their properties, governed by rules such as hadronic interactions and the strong nuclear force, can be extensively studied, providing valuable insights into their behavior under different conditions, ultimately shedding light on their internal quark-gluon makeup. This understanding can then be applied to related areas, like the study of heavy-ion collisions at various energy levels, to better comprehend the properties of heavy nuclei.

Unmanned Aerial Vehicles, or UAVs, have become a significant part of modern warfare, with various countries utilizing them in military operations. Literature analysis reveals a crucial role of swarm UAVs in future conflicts, necessitating a deeper examination of their military applications. By examining 1,185 research papers on military UAV swarms, a NLP-based analysis uncovers 414 drivers of development, comprising 0.3% irrelevant entries and 71.5% commercial interests. The findings highlight the growing influence of private companies, such as Google, Microsoft, and Uber, on military UAV research. The results show that specific UAV swarm drivers, such as communication, sensing, and locomotion, dominate discussions, while others, like targeting, remain underexplored. The study's methodology serves as a model for NLP-based assessments of other military technologies.

When performing cosmological inferences based on the Lyman-$\alpha$ correlation functions, standard analyses usually only consider a specific dimension. Our work now includes cross-correlations between different two-dimensional slices to make more use of the data. This leads to improved model constraints and a clearer distinction between the information contained in one-dimensional correlations and that contained in their cross-dimensional counterparts. Our findings suggest that including these additional dimensions leads to higher precision in determining key cosmological parameters, even when using a simple model. This result highlights the full potential of the Lyman-$\alpha$ data for making precise cosmological inferences.

Researchers at Fermilab have successfully conducted an experiment where a beam of particles undergoes an unconventional manipulation, swapping its horizontal and longitudinal beam patterns at the A0 Photoinjector. The new experimental setup, featuring a specially designed deflector followed by a curved waveguide, has enabled the first observation of a distinct phase shift between the particle beam's trajectory and its time-of-flight.

This paper presents a novel research in behavior prediction, a core aspect of the social behavior models used to create realistic agent behaviors in various applications such as autonomous driving and animation. We observe that existing prediction methods focus on the past history of a subject, but neglect the future outcomes, resulting in predicted trajectories that are statically connected to the history. To address this issue, we introduce a novel technique, Sliding Sequential CVAE (SSCVAE), that dynamically considers both the past history and the future predictions in a sliding window. The SSCVAE model incorporates a socially-aware factor to optimize the model and evaluates the performance using multiple metrics on two publicly available datasets.

Over the past thirty years, various theoretical models have been introduced to analyze intricate systems. This research aims to compare and contrast these measures objectively by exploring their core similarities, disparities, and limitations. To achieve this goal, artificial neural networks, known as Boltzmann machines, are employed as a unified framework to examine the predictive capabilities of these measures. By systematically varying key parameters of randomly generated machines, the predictive performances are evaluated using diverse system configurations, and the outcomes are quantitatively measured using various complexity metrics. Our findings indicate that certain network characteristics are indispensable for proficient prediction, and the capacity for these measures to forecast structured patterns within a system can serve as a benchmark for evaluating their effectiveness. Furthermore, the research identifies correlations and disparities between these measures, demonstrating that some metrics outperform others in predicting structured patterns.

This paper outlines our current advancements in the area of human-swarm
interaction, focusing on the underlying technology required for efficient
and effective communication between swarms of robots and humans. We are
exploring decentralized human gesture recognition using centralised machine
learning models, which will enable swarm navigation and control. Our goal is
to enable natural communication between humans and swarms of robots, which
will have a range of practical applications across multiple disciplines.

The study aims to assess the performance of composite deep learning models consisting of Recurrent Neural Networks and Convolutional Neural Networks for identifying diverse White Blood Cell types, a feat that could revolutionize automated medical diagnosis and blood analysis in pharmaceutical and healthcare settings by analyzing image samples, thereby aiding in disease diagnosis for patients.

A key advantage of counterdiabatic protocols in driving quantum states involves the use of a supporting, auxiliary gauge potential. However, determining this potential requires the full Hamiltonian, posing a challenge for preparing ground states in complex systems. A new approach, termed variational counterdiabatic, is proposed in this context. This method, derived using perturbation theory, allows for the gauge potential to be approximated using perturbative terms of the Hamiltonian. Employing this approach to drive a Hubbard model parametrically, it is demonstrated that it is possible to achieve fast and smooth state preparation, even when using a linear driving protocol. A key advantage of this method is its insensitivity to the choice of initial parameters, a benefit not shared by other driving techniques. A general strategy is also outlined for designing and optimizing the driving trajectory to prepare ground states.

Color neutrality is a critical aspect of any image representation. This property is essential for various image processing tasks like image enhancement, compression, and recognition, as it prevents color information from misleading these operations. In various image representation techniques, including multi-spectral images, color images can be converted into a single channel representation to maintain color consistency and reduce metadata size. However, standard methods fail to preserve the original color tone of images, resulting in a significant loss of critical information for image interpretation. In this study, we introduce an innovative, fast image decolorization approach, based on analysis of luminance and temperature patterns. This simple yet efficient technique successfully captures the essence of color distribution in an image, producing a monochromatic representation faithful to the original color tone. We compare our method with other leading techniques, demonstrating its superior performance both quantitatively and qualitatively.

This research develops an expression to calculate the coefficients of the Taylor series of e raised to a variable that takes a complex value, utilizing an iterative formula which enables the computation of each coefficient to be dependent on previous ones, in contrast to other methods where the calculation of one coefficient can rely solely on the previous one, thus eliminating the potential for parallel computation. As an alternative to the complex exponential Taylor series, we also derive an expression for a similar series of the complex logarithm, with the iterative formula now relying on a recursive relation involving two previous coefficients. Both the exponential and logarithm series can be generalized to functions of arbitrary variables with mixed real and complex components.

Given a surface S equipped with a metric d, such that it meets the conditions set by Alexandrov for an upper curvature bound, we demonstrate that an almost conformal harmonic map from a surface to the pair (S, d) results in a branched covering. Consequently, if (S, d) is topologically equivalent to the two-dimensional sphere S^2, it then becomes conformally equivalent to S^2.

We've created a state-of-the-art laser-plasma platform to study fundamental photon-photon collision phenomena, such as the linear Breit-Wheeler process, using laser wakefield acceleration and a high-energy gamma-ray beam. To test its capabilities, we conducted an experiment focusing on the production of electron-positron pairs using a 20 GeV gamma-ray beam, generated by a self-standing gamma-ray source, in interaction with a high-density plasma target. Our results demonstrate the feasibility of using a laser-plasma system for photon-photon collisions, offering a promising way to access Breit-Wheeler physics with high-energy gamma-ray beams, as well as offering a viable alternative to traditional particle colliders.

Two-Higgs Doublet Models, especially those with type-II favourisation due to $CP$-conserving and breaking properties, are examined in the context of the LHC's search for additional radiation. A focus is placed on the lightest CP-eigenstate $h$, with suppression of $hgg$ production and detection predicted when the second doublet vev is negligible, under a specific alignment condition. However, the implementation of a soft-breaking $Z_2$ parameter, $m_{12}$, introduces a crucial uncertainty in the $h$ coupling to bosons during tree-level simulations, with the two models' predictions diverging in these interactions. This $Z_2$ parameter's influence is further observed in the lightest pseudoscalar boson $a$ interactions with fermions, with a proposed approach for incorporating $m_{12}$ into the Two-Higgs Doublet Models considered. A study of the LHC's predicted search results for $h$ in association with a light, undetected pseudoscalar boson $a$, with simultaneous consideration of the background and $hgg$ signal uncertainties in this scenario is presented, using the LHC at $\sqrt{s}=13$ TeV and with 300 fb$^{-1}$ data input. This leads to the derivation of conservative bounds for the $m_{12}$ parameter, with the type-II, $CP$-conserving and breaking Two-Higgs Doublet Model predictions displaying the lowest sensitivity

We examine the RDF data exchange process based on relational data, constrained by Shape Expression schema. Our research involves addressing critical issues, including determining feasibility for source data and identifying optimal target schemas. With the capacity to incorporate null values, existing solutions to RDF data exchange are rendered unreliable. By extending existing work, we develop novel methods to handle Shape Expression schema sourcing and target schema evaluation. Our approach differs from prior work due to the inclusion of Shape Expression semantics and null value considerations.

A new field known as shape-based convex regression has recently emerged, focusing on the identification of a globally optimal solution for a specific type of convex function through optimization. This function, used in the implementation of a non-linear mixed-effect model in the field of economics, has been found to be beneficial in generating a cloud of possible solutions instead of a single definitive answer. The shape-based convex regression approach is versatile and can be used in various fields such as medicine, economics, and biology. A recent paper introduced a new method known as StoNED, utilizing a mix of trace norm and entropic regularization to create a convex and differentiable function. This paper provides an in-depth review of the implementation details of the StoNED algorithm, offering a step-by-step guide on the implementation process. A new Python package named pyStoNED has been created to facilitate the use of the StoNED algorithm, including a step-by-step guide on the implementation process.

In a study based on the 13 TeV LHC dataset, we investigate the interplay between the lightest Higgs boson observed and the top quark's quantum states. The focus of our research lies in understanding how the top quark's quantum states influence searches for the 125 GeV Higgs boson in conjunction with the top quark. The basis of our investigation is informed by the Standard Model's predictions that account for the effects of both neutrino pairs and single leptons resulting from the semi-leptonic decay of the top quark. The simulated dataset used in our research includes the inclusive $t\bar t\phi$ production mode. The distinction between signal and background was determined by a fit to the dataset, yielding an estimated upper limit for the inclusive production mode. The results of our research indicate that experiments focusing solely on neutrino pairs have failed to detect the Higgs boson up to masses of approximately 15 GeV. The upper limits obtained in our research are comparable to those reported in experiments focusing solely on leptons. The influence of the top quark's quantum states, particularly in the decay of the top quark into lepton pairs, has been found to be negligible in determining the upper limits for the Higgs boson's mass.

Pre-trained language models possess the ability to capture syntactic information, as established in previous studies [Tenney et al., 2019, Jawahar et al., 2019, Hewitt and Manning, 2019]. This work presents two unsupervised constituency parsing systems, one relying on syntactic biases in pre-trained language models and the other utilizing co-training to estimate parse trees. These systems, being efficient and small, can also benefit from the strengths of contemporary few-shot learning techniques. As a result, we present two innovative approaches: generating pseudo annotations via few-shot learning and adapting parsing models to pseudo annotations. Our extensive evaluation on 9 languages across 3 domains demonstrates the superior performance of our models, particularly their ability to handle low-resource languages and scenarios with limited data.

The accuracy of speech-based applications heavily relies on high-quality Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR). Despite having access to advanced ASR tools, the lack of sufficient training data for languages other than English severely hampers progress in these fields. Kaldi, a widely-used open-source ASR tool, has been limited in its capabilities to support non-English languages due to its closed-source training data limitations. Our research focuses on leveraging Kaldi's capacity for in-data training, thereby eliminating the need for external data sets. Our contributions include a detailed dataset analysis of the Kaldi-German-WS dataset and comparisons with state-of-the-art ASR models. Additionally, we explore the potential for enhancing Kaldi's training accuracy by incorporating supplementary data sources. Our findings indicate that the Kaldi-German-WS dataset is the most advanced open-source training data currently available for German speech data, representing up to 1,500 hours of speech. Our model trained from this data outperforms a Kaldi model trained without any language-specific data, reducing the word error rate by 35%. This development has significant implications for speech-based applications in German, opening up new avenues for research in the field.

The origin of Be-type stars is still unclear with theories involving both single and coeval star formations that may involve distinct pathways. To explore this issue, researchers studied Be stars within the 30 Doradus star cluster using Hubble Space Telescope data. By analyzing spectral images from the Wide Field Camera 3, the study identified 13 Be stars, all of which are or are expected to be blue straggler stars. The research found that these Be stars are significantly brighter than non-Be B stars of similar mass within the cluster. The study also discovered that Be stars exhibit greater mass loss and faster rotation than non-Be B stars of comparable mass. The research found that mass loss rates for Be stars in the 30 Doradus cluster are lower than those found in the SMC and SMC-like environments but higher than those found in the GMC N11B. The research found that Be-type stars in the 30 Doradus cluster have slower rotation speeds than those found in the SMC. The research found that Be-type stars in the 30 Doradus cluster have lower v/sin(I) values than non-Be B stars of comparable mass. The research found that Be-type stars in the 30 Doradus cluster have lower projected rotation speeds than those found in the SMC.
