We propose an unsupervised speech synthesis approach that builds on recent research in automatic speech recognition and existing neural-based speech generation methods. Employing only raw, unlabeled audio and text data, as well as a dictionary, our technique enables high-quality speech synthesis without requiring a prelabeled dataset. Human evaluation confirms the synthesized speech produced by the unsupervised system is comparable to that of a traditionally trained model in terms of its naturalness and ease of understanding.

This work investigates how the Tsallis holographic dark energy model behaves with a complex quintessence field. We derive constraints on the model's parameters by fitting the model to the most recent data from Hubble parameters, leading to findings that are somewhat at odds with those of another study on quintessence fields. We also examine the model's ability to explain certain cosmological features, such as a transition in the universe's expansion history and anomalies in the large-scale structure. These investigations aim to leave open the possibility that the universe has undergone a period of decelerated expansion.

Multi-objective mixed-integer non-linear programming problems frequently arise in real-world contexts, notably in mechanical engineering. A novel approach, combining multi-criteria decision-making and branch-and-bound, is proposed for solving such problems. A detailed description of the proposed method is provided, incorporating a non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm II and an implementation example. Comparative results demonstrate that this hybrid approach surpasses traditional optimization methods and contemporary multi-objective algorithms.

The internal connection and integration principles in a synthetic differential geometry setting are crucial concepts in differentiating manifolds and Lie groupoids. This paper redefines these principles within this framework, then demonstrates that a specific condition - being a connected Lie groupoid - implies internal connectivity and integration.

The Dynaswap project focuses on developing a robust, trustworthy architecture for safeguarding digital biomaterials. This framework builds on existing network capabilities, drawing on experience from the advanced bioinformatics network infrastructure. Dynaswap's architecture leverages a dynamic, distributed model to manage and display digital content, incorporating cutting-edge virtualization and container technologies to ensure seamless interaction with local systems. In addition, Dynaswap centers around user-centric, intuitive interfaces for sharing and accessing sensitive materials securely. In our research, we present the current state of Dynaswap's development and evaluate user perceptions and system performance. Our evaluation assesses various aspects, such as the impact of sharing sensitive data on user trust in sharing platforms, the performance of content dissemination, and the processing efficiency of content display.

Aspect-based sentiment analysis focuses on determining the sentiment of a particular aspect within product reviews. Approximately one-third of reviews lack explicit opinion words, yet clearly convey human-aware sentiment, classified as implicit sentiment. We propose a supervised pre-training approach to capture implicit sentiment for the first time in this field. Our method, CSAP, leverages an innovative supervised contrastive pre-training objective to extract implicit sentiment from annotated data. CSAP employs a two-stage architecture that separates the encoding of both the review and aspect and the extraction of implicit sentiment from the aspects. We implement a new objective called aspect-review similarity, which highlights implicit sentiment phrases within reviews. For the second stage, we introduce a contrastive learning objective to refine the model's representation of aspects and extract implicit sentiment. We evaluate our approach on six datasets from the ATSEM dataset collection. CSAP achieves state-of-the-art results, outperforming existing approaches by 2.11% on average in aspect-specific sentiment analysis tasks.

We explore how to analyze data from case-control studies using mediation analysis, especially when we have information about a binary mediator. Our method involves creating pseudo-control groups to estimate the effect of key variables, which we show can be based on the same parameters as the study's logistic model. We test these methods on real-world data and show that they provide reliable estimates, even with small sample sizes. Notably, our approach allows us to assess the effect of certain variables, like the odds of having a certain disease in a population, without requiring individual-level data.

This research delves into secure communication systems for multiple users that utilize reconfigurable intelligent surfaces to compensate for hardware limitations.
We develop mixed-integer non-linear programs to optimize these systems, focusing on maximizing secrecy rates and minimizing average transmission power.
Our designs separate signal transmission and RIS beam-forming, reducing complexity while maintaining stability and robustness despite hardware impairments.
Comparisons with conventional methods demonstrate significant performance enhancements, particularly in scenarios with hardware limitations.

We begin by defining a task for few-shot continual learning, which necessitates constantly acquiring and updating new classifications without prior knowledge of their distribution. A proposed solution is the Resampling Relabeling Executor (RRE), which achieves this goal by leveraging an executive module responsible for selecting relevant past experiences as training references. The RRE executive module then employs contrastive value policy to identify and exploit the most relevant past memories, which are then used to train a new on a reduced set of data, relabeling the perceptions through hindsight summary to facilitate knowledge transfer.

We studied the solar wind energy flux near the sun using data from the Parker Solar Probe's first 13 months of operation. Two techniques were employed to analyze data from the Proton Sensor on the spacecraft. The first approach involved using a parameter called Poyttinger flux to estimate energy flux, while the second method utilized the distribution of proton velocities to calculate energy flux. Both techniques yielded similar results. The average energy flux decreased as we moved closer to the sun, averaging around 1.340x10^3 W/m^2. The distribution of energy flux values followed a 1/r^2 pattern, suggesting that different solar regions contribute unevenly to the energy flux. The observed energy flux values matched predictions based on current solar models and matched the energy flux measured near the sun in 1976, but the current rates are lower than expected based on theory alone. The lower-than-expected energy flux may be due to a phenomenon where magnetic fields are weakening the solar convective zone.

In a noncommutative setting, where locally compact Hausdorff groups act on C*-algebras, we introduce the concept of a numerable principal bundle with quantum characteristics. This generalization involves defining a locally trivial G-C*-algebra as a noncommutative analog to the total space of a numerable principal bundle. By employing the spectrum's homeomorphism, which is invariant under the group's action, we identify a suitable locally compact Hausdororff space as the noncommutative counterpart to the base space of the bundle. The action of G on C*-algebras enables the construction of a noncommutative analog to transition functions, which demonstrate a cocycle relationship. The total space, consisting of these transition functions, constitutes a noncommutative principal bundle if specific conditions, including separability and quasifree properties, are met.

We show that any family of maximal almost-disjoint sets can be eliminated via a specific method that preserves the properties of a certain minimal structure, resulting in the equality $w_1=\mathcal{a}$. It's also demonstrated that any ultrafilter $\mathcal{U}$ can be extended to a selective free ultrafilter $\mathcal{F}$ of the same properties, resulting in $\mathcal{U} <_\mathcal{F} <_\mathcal{F}^* \mathcal{F}$ with $\mathcal{F}^*$ selective. Furthermore, it's proven that any free ideal $I$ can be embedded into a free ideal $J$ such that $I <_S J^*$, where $J^*$ is a selective free ideal.

We've developed a new approach to optomechanics by initially examining a $q$-deformed optomechanical system. This approach leads to modified optical properties. In this study, we explore the transmission of light passing through an optomechanical cavity with experiments and theoretical simulations. Our results show that the system's behavior can be altered by means of the $q$-deformation parameter. We have identified and analyzed enhancements in light amplification within the system. Additionally, we have explored the possibility of amplification in subluminous light speeds in optomechanics for the first time.

In a previous study, I developed a model where the Two-Rotors Model's negative scissors states, consisting of two-sided classical bodies, exhibited 1 |K| = 1; 0 components and negative space parity. Building on this work, I explored reflections of intrinsic collective modes with negative R-parity. Incorporating these reflections into the 1 |K| = 1; 0 component resulted in a multimaximum distribution of classical bodies, characteristic of the negative scissors mode. Calculations of transition energies and B(E2) values indicated that the two-sided nature of the negative scissors mode is consistent with experimental constraints. Furthermore, I investigated how reflections might influence the degeneracy of the 1 |K| = 1; 0 component and negative  |K| = 1; 1 components, ultimately demonstrating that reflections could account for the experimental degeneracy through a mixing mechanism.

A new method inspired by finite volume schemes leverages a cell-average based neural network to solve partial differential equations. By utilizing the weak formulation of these equations, the method trains a neural network to accurately predict solution values at a cellular level, maintaining stability through a suitable under-relaxation technique. Initially developed for first-order hyperbolic equations, the approach has been expanded to include second-order equations, as well as semi-conductive transport phenomena. Furthermore, the method can be applied to linear and nonlinear equations, and is compatible with a range of numerical techniques, including the use of upwind fluxes and diverse numerical quadrature methods.

The ALICE Collaboration has been chosen to upgrade its experiment at the LHC, with the goal of collecting data on the Pb-P collisions at the LHC's highest energy level from 2025 to 2029. An opportunity has arisen for the collaboration to begin utilizing the LHC's full energy range of 6.5 TeV per A per collision during Run 3 from 2021 to 2025. Building on this success, the ALICE Upgrade will take advantage of cutting-edge technologies in advanced electronics and sensor technology to create a next-generation experiment. A key component of the experiment will be two specialized detectors: the Forward Detectors and the Trigger Detectors. These innovative devices will be compact, robust, and high-tech, representing a significant advancement in particle physics research. A special feature of the experiment will be its ability to record data on the Pb-P collisions at an unprecedented 100 kHz rate, with the goal of studying rare physical phenomena. Additionally, the experiment will have the capability to begin utilizing the LHC's full energy range during Run 3, with the goal of studying the Pb-P collisions at an unprecedented 6.5 TeV per A per collision. An experimental plan has been proposed for Run 3, with the goal of studying the Pb-P collisions at multiple energy levels, including 5.2 TeV per A per collision during standard data collection and up to 13 TeV per A per collision during specialized LHC runs. An innovative data-taking

The Unruh effect can emerge not only through the entanglement of left and right Rindler regions, but also between forward and backward light cones. Our analysis focuses on the geometric phase arising from this time-related entanglement between the future and past, showing that it can be effectively modelled by a $\Lambda$-system. The work provides a proposal for an experiment that might enable the timelike Unruh effect to be detected through quantum teleportation.

One of the primary objectives of Information Extraction involves recognizing event descriptions along with their related components within a given text. This task has received significant research attention, yet efforts focused on non-English languages remain largely underrepresented due to a lack of quality datasets required for effective model development and evaluation. To fill this gap, we have developed a Multilingual Event Extraction dataset featuring detailed English descriptions of events, their associated entities, and quoted original texts in multiple languages. This dataset enables accurate comparison of English-based models with those designed for non-English languages, presenting new challenges and opportunities for further exploration.

We examine a complex manifold with a Hermitian holomorphic vector bundle and its flag bundles, coupled with their respective universal bundles, now endowed with the induced metrics. The key point involves proving positivity of their Chern forms for use in pushing forward to the base manifold, ultimately leading to evaluation of key integrals and point count information via local contributions, specifically in relation to Grauert's theorem.

Observations from multiple spacecraft have investigated the behavior of the stellar companion in high-mass X-ray binaries, but their findings regarding the wind's impact on the wind from the companion star are mixed. New research has analyzed data from INTEGRAL, Swift, and Suzaku to simulate how the wind from the companion star in Cyg X-1 would affect the geometry of the primary star's accretion disk. Analyzing this effect in the hard state of Cyg X-1, the researchers found that the wind from the companion star significantly alters the primary star's accretion disk, causing it to become elongated in the direction of the companion star. This modification results in the presence of extended wings in the spectral lines emitted by the primary star, which may explain previous discrepancies in the wind's impact on the wind from the companion star in high-mass X-ray binaries. The researchers' model also predicts that the wind from the companion star would compress the primary star's accretion disk in the direction perpendicular to the companion star's orbit, an effect that could be confirmed by future large-scale space missions.

The Yang-Mills-aether theory is analyzed to understand the implications of introducing non-abelian aether-like terms that violate Lorentz symmetry, specifically within thermal quantum field theory. By incorporating temperature effects and spatial compactification via Thermofield Dynamics, corrections to the non-abelian Stefan-Boltzmann law and non-abelian Casimir energy and pressure are calculated for both zero and finite temperatures.

Researchers have long sought to bridge the gap between syntax and semantics parsing but so far have had to make a choice between excelling in one area at the cost of the other, contradicting research highlighting the complex interactions between the two systems. This paper presents a novel approach that simultaneously parses syntax and semantics by representing a common underlying structure shared by a mother tongue. An experimental analysis within a cross-lingual context reveals commonalities and contrasts in the syntax and semantics of 9 languages, and demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed model using data from the BEA 2019 shared task. Our findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the interactions between syntax and semantics parsing, and the proposed model achieves state-of-the-art performance in simultaneous parsing.

The formation of magnetically-driven jets from accretion disks following a binary neutron star merger is studied using computer simulations. The analysis reveals that jets forming from disks cooled by neutrino emission are more powerful and dense than those developing from disks with neutron star cooling. The outflows' properties are independent of the magnetorotational instability activity, within the simulation's scope. The proposed model is expected to contribute to a deeper understanding of postmerger disk behavior and the jet launching process, ultimately shedding light on various astrophysical phenomena such as short duration gamma ray bursts and kilonovae.

We utilized data from the Hyper Suprime-Cam Subaru Strategic Program to analyze a sample of 3849 massive elliptical galaxies at a redshift of 0.3-0.9. Our research involved examining their tidal features and finding a strong correlation between the galaxies' robustness and the percentage of debris visible. The results are consistent with simulations indicating that intense tidal forces lead to significant loss of mass, which in turn affects the galaxies' mass. Additionally, our findings suggest that simulated data match observations when taking into account the impact of dust on tidal features. The estimated annual merger rates for galaxies of our study's mass range are 0.18-0.33 per 100,000 square megaparsecs, which aligns with predictions from simulations. The significant presence of tidal features in our study's massive galaxy sample implies that these galaxies' robustness results, in part, from weak interactions with smaller companion galaxies.

The Azimuthally Symmetric Theory of Gravitation (ASTG) was previously shown to provide an explanation for unidirectional plasma outflows in various celestial objects. This paper offers a detailed mathematical description of outflow geometry, based on a solution derived from ASTG that has a toroidal shape. The derivation of ASTG's repulsive gravitational force for small-scale objects near the outflow source is also presented, using a first-order approximation for simplicity. A comparison of derived outflow characteristics with observed features of the jet-like outflows from Jupiter's North Pole and the Galactic Center is included.

We have gathered a vast dataset of observations during and following fast radio bursts, making it the largest compilation to date. Our research incorporates a combination of observations, consisting of those made simultaneously or shortly after the event, as well as follow-up observations in various wavelengths. Theoretical models suggest that FRBs occur in the radio quiet environment of the galactic halo or the intergalactic medium. Our findings from optical surveys like the Very Large Telescope, the Hubble Space Telescope, and the Kepler telescope indicate a lack of emission in the optical range during and following FRBs. Theoretical expectations indicate that the optical flux of FRBs decreases rapidly with distance, which is why FRBs from far-distant galaxies may be detectable only in the optical range. Our research reveals an upper limit on the Delay-Optical Flux Ratio of 8.5e21, which is similar to the previously measured upper limit of 3e21.

The combination of chirped pulse amplification and nonlinear optical systems has been the foundation of significant technological advancements over the past three decades. Consequently, many contemporary high-power laser facilities are driven by optical systems that balance numerous trade-offs, including power, efficiency, size, and reliability. The application of analytical tools, such as engineering approximations and numerical models, has enabled researchers to design, optimize, and understand these complex systems. This work presents an overview of these analytical tools, emphasizing recent advances in numerical modeling. The paper specifically focuses on three critical aspects of high-power laser design: optimizing nonlinear amplification, managing beam propagation, and balancing thermal load and damage risk in the pump pump laser. Furthermore, the paper showcases numerical models developed for the analysis and reverse engineering of historical laser systems, an approach that is essential for the ongoing design and improvement of future high-power laser facilities.

Multimodal language generation capabilities of models like GPT-2 and GPT-3 can be leveraged for producing high-quality text, but can also be utilized for creating visual controls like selecting options in dropdown menus within chat interfaces. This research introduces the first attempt at fine-tuning pre-trained language models to produce text-based instructions that enable visual interactions, allowing for the selection of options within a simulated dropdown menu. By incorporating image and layout processing capabilities from UNIMELB's vision-language model PRETRAIN-MLS, the model can be equipped with the ability to control visual elements with keyboard events, enabling a seamless user experience. This innovative approach enables language models to produce complex, multifaceted user inputs that go beyond traditional text-based communication.

We introduce an upgraded RingCT protocol that supports stealth addresses in conjunction with Delegated Proof of Stake, resulting in Delegated RingCT.
The Delegated RingCT scheme comprises two main components: an extended public key encoding system for secret spending and a one-way hash transformation for fast and light transactions.
A detailed security analysis is performed to ensure that the proposed scheme meets the required security standards, including indistinguishability of parallel and sequential hash outputs and existential unforgeability of transaction signatures.
Our experiments demonstrate that Delegated RingCT offers a significant increase in transaction processing speed while maintaining anonymity, outperforming previous RingCT and FairCoin prototypes.

In 2015, CERN introduced "Emittance Scans," a new fast luminosity separation scanning method at the Large Hadron Collider. These scans were consistently carried out during physics production runs, utilizing full-intensity beams at the CMS experiment's interaction point. The emittance scans allowed for the simultaneous measurement of beam properties and closed orbits at the level of individual bunches, without disrupting particle collisions. The first successful emittance scans were implemented, providing novel data on long-range beam-beam effects, as predicted by models such as Touschek scattering and head-tail instabilities.

Recent breakthroughs in artificial neural networks have accelerated the development of data-driven modeling in science, engineering, and technology. This paper outlines various cooperative strategies for training artificial neural networks, highlighting their advantages over traditional training methods. By employing cooperative training, network generalization can be improved, reduced sampling error can reveal underlying data patterns, and realistic noise can be injected for enhanced uncertainty estimation and anomaly detection. Real-world applications in meteorology, computer vision, and medical diagnostics serve as examples of the practical significance of cooperative data-driven modeling.

This research examines the decay processes $\Upsilon(10753)\to \Upsilon(nS)\pi^+\pi^-$. As this transition is not allowed for hadronic decays of quarkonia, it's a prime example of physics beyond the Standard Model. We investigate the four-body decay of $\Upsilon(10753)$ via a hadronic loop mechanism, exploring its potential to explain the $\Upsilon(10753)$ state. We've calculated the production rates for $\Upsilon(10753)\to \Upsilon(2S)\pi^+\pi^-,$ $\Upsilon(10753)\to \Upsilon(1S)\pi^+\pi^-,$ and $\Upsilon(10753)\to \Upsilon(3S)\pi^+\pi^-$. The results suggest that the first process might be observable at Belle II, while the other two are not.

We've developed a novel optimization technique, AskewSGD, to train large neural networks with quantized weights to reduce memory and speed up processing. Unlike other approaches that either rely on gradient analysis or assume invariance, AskewSGD is a generalized method that constrains optimization within valid quantized ranges and adapts to the network's dynamics. By slowly relaxing these constraints, our method achieves significant performance improvement while maintaining efficiency. AskewSGD is a generalized method that can be applied with various optimization algorithms, allowing for high flexibility. When combined with Stochastic Gradient Descent, it yields high performance and efficient training on deep neural networks with 8-bit weights, achieving similar accuracy to 32-bit weight networks while training much faster.

The Continuum Soft Robotics project's third edition gathers experts from various fields to illustrate the progression and difficulties in creating intelligent robotic systems. This project's objectives are to assemble a comprehensive collection of preliminary papers, foster discussion, and pinpoint obstacles in developing innovative robotic technologies. As part of CSR, we undertook a detailed examination of previous research in developing control systems for flexible robotic arms. In this work, we summarize the current state of this research, highlight specific challenges, and offer a comprehensive list of difficulties in this area, thus contributing to the CSR project.

The Jacobi group $G^J(\mathbb{R})$ is typically defined as a combination of the real circle group $S^1$ and the Heisenberg group $\mathbb{R} 2+\mathbb{Z}$, with the standard action of $\mathbb{Z}$ on $S^1$. However, this definition leads to a non-nilpotent group which is unusual and poses difficulties in investigations. Alternatively, we define the real Jacobi group $G^J(\mathbb{R})$ as a combination of the real circle group $S^1$ and the affine group $G_1(\mathbb{R})$ of $\mathbb{R}$, resulting in a nilpotent group that is a direct product of two nilpotent groups and possesses interesting representations, with a focus on their structure and characteristic subgroups.

Verifying facts using structured data can be difficult, necessitating a model's
understanding of both language and symbolic computations involving data in
tables. Despite pre-trained language models excelling in confirming simple
assertions, they often falter when handling complex assertions requiring
multiple calculations. In our research, we alleviate this challenge by breaking
down intricate assertions into manageable sub-problems. By employing a unique
split-and-hope strategy, we assess the potential solutions to each part and
amass a final answer from the hopeful contributions. Our computational tests
demonstrate the efficacy of this data-driven decomposition method on fact-checking
tasks across three diverse domains: (1) a database of US laws, (2) a database
of hospital information, and (3) a collection of COVID-19 statistics.

The state of the art in learned synthetic image generation involves generative adversarial networks. Initial breakthroughs in the field relied on unsupervised images generation, generating images directly from raw input. More recently, the focus has shifted to conditioned images generation, where GANs generate images based on specific data such as scene masks or object positions. This allows for images creation with set objects or in specific locations within a scene. This thesis explores the challenges in developing this type of images conditioning for GANs and evaluates different approaches to achieve this goal. By applying various techniques to map scenes into a shared visual space, the results demonstrate the feasibility of the proposed methods. Latent space conditioning is then utilized to generate images that represent a scene from a specific viewpoint or orientation, similar to generating images from object masks.

To perform Bayesian inference using nested sampling, a specific prior sampling approach called slice sampling is commonly utilized. However, slice sampling's performance can be heavily influenced by the complex geometry of the parameter space, leading to inefficient sampling that delays or entirely halts the nested sampling analysis. As an alternative, researchers have developed "step sampler" algorithms to move prior samples towards more informative regions of the space, enhancing the nested sampling analysis. We have implemented and evaluated three step samplers - generalised step, generalised winding, and a novel adaptation of the gradient winding step sampler - within the Wyithe nested sampling implementation. We have conducted a series of experiments on a range of benchmark and real-world Bayesian models to measure the performance of these step sampler algorithms in enhancing the efficiency of nested sampling analyses.

In fault-tolerant distance labelling, we're tasked with assigning brief descriptions to the points in a network so that knowing any three points' labels allows us to deduce the direct distance between any two of them, excluding the third. Our work proves that any weighted network with a specific layout (or in fact any network with limited separating elements) allows the assignment of brief descriptions with a specific length, that enables the inference of distances in networks with one element failing. Additionally, we show that these descriptions can be selected so that the labels assigned to nearby elements have similar lengths.

In this study, we investigate two-particle correlations in time and frequency for a Bose-Hubbard model subject to external driving and dissipation, focusing particularly on a quasi-one-dimensional chain. We find that two-particle correlations in time exhibit distinct oscillations, influenced by nearest-neighbor interactions, which can be accurately described using a mean-field Bose-Hubbard model. Conversely, frequency-domain correlations reveal a more intricate structure, characterized by a complex interplay of single-particle and multi-particle excitations. Utilizing a many-body T-matrix approach, which is exact in the weak-dissipation limit, we are able to derive a complete understanding of the interaction spectrum. We find that for significant nearest-neighbor interactions, the interaction spectrum significantly deviates from the well-known approximation derived from mean-field theory. Furthermore, we identify distinct bounds to the interaction spectrum that can be derived from a mean-field Bose-Hubbard model with complex-valued parameters. We also observe that the interaction spectrum exhibits a shift towards positive values as dissipation increases.

For a given second-order linear elliptic equation with coefficients $A$, $\mathbf{b}$ and a parameter $\lambda$, defined within a bounded $\mathbb{R}^2$ domain $\Omega$ and satisfying specific smoothness and boundedness conditions, we establish existence and uniqueness of the weak solution in $W^{1,p}_0(\Omega)$ for the Dirichlet problem, where $2<p<\infty$, assuming that the equation also includes source terms in $L^2(\Omega)$.

Recent advancements in machine learning have allowed approaches other than decision boundary analysis to be overlooked, specifically the study of in- and out-of-distribution data classification. This study focuses on out-of-distribution detection, a critical component of reliable machine learning, where a model identifies data not consistent with any known classification learned during training. Current methods utilizing deep Gaussian processes have shown promise but are hampered by computational issues affecting their training and validation times. We propose a novel solution by splitting the Gaussian process pipeline into smaller, faster-to-compute parts, allowing for more efficient detection. We test our approach's ability to detect out-of-distribution data generated by a mixture of two Gaussian distributions, exhibiting improved performance compared to existing baselines.

Quantum systems driven periodically experience heat buildup due to resonant wave-packet trajectories visiting higher energy states, but by using a controlled heat flow in one dimension, Bose condensation can form in the resulting "scarred" states, preserving the thermal dynamics while stabilizing the condensate. This concept is illustrated with an optical-lattice system that uses photons from an extended optical design.

The article explores the convex solution $u$ of the Monge--Amp\`ere equation in an open convex domain with a nonnegative, bounded right-hand side, along with specific boundary data. A key finding relates Alexandrov's maximum principle, specifically its equivalence to H\"older continuity, for convex solutions of this equation. Furthermore, the solutions can be shown to exhibit uniform H\"older continuity, with the constant depending solely on the $W^{1,p}$ norm of the right-hand side and selected positive parameters.

Counting the recurrence of periodic events allows us to measure time. Historically, developing stable and accurate timekeeping devices was a significant undertaking. We will instead examine a different class of timekeeping devices, based on random clicking mechanisms. A comprehensive statistical analysis reveals the limitations and complexities of these devices, particularly in their ability to synchronize with a shared time reference. Notably, even with ideal synchronization, these devices can exhibit significant inaccuracies, particularly in their ability to record time in a continuous manner. We will also explore the theoretical boundaries of accuracy and precision based on fundamental principles of probability theory.

This research introduces an innovative approach to managing service flows in distributed networks by integrating software techniques and network infrastructure. The proposed framework, which incorporates resource management, fault avoidance, and fault recovery in the face of component failures, is designed to ensure real-time service delivery. The framework's key features include a service model that accounts for failure risks, an algorithm that schedules service components based on performance and power consumption, a fault detection system that uses data from network devices, a prevention mechanism that blocks failed nodes from service flow composition, and a recovery mechanism that reconfigures service flows and resource allocation to maintain service quality. Simulation results demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed approach under various failure scenarios validate its value in ensuring timely service delivery and optimal resource utilization.

Metric learning's pair-wise loss technique is centered around optimizing an embedding that maximizes similarity between images within the same class, while minimizing similarities between images in different classes. Various forms of pair-wise loss strategies have been proposed. To consolidate this diverse range of loss functions, we've isolated specific aspects that dictate how these functions operate, and then categorize them into four distinct groups. By examining the effects of these groups, we've developed 'gradient surgery', a method that allows us to surgically combine different gradient dynamics into a single optimization algorithm. Our method enables optimal optimization, and our experiments show that a simple algorithm designed with gradient surgery can surpass the performance of state-of-the-art techniques, particularly in retrieval tasks.

In this context, we explore certain classes of quantum codes that can be efficiently constructed in the lattice gauge theory framework known as holographic tensor network. By establishing a precise relationship between their computational and storage capacities, we are able to pinpoint the maximum achievable ratio for these codes. The optimal coding rates we derive are directly proportional to the square of the ratio between the inverse critical temperature and the C-scale, a characteristic length dimensionless proportionality constant. The maximum coding rates we obtain through AdS geometry predictions are in agreement with the theoretical limit established by the holographic entropy bound. The efficacy of these codes is further substantiated by their ability to correct errors of orders proportional to the logarithm of the total entropy. Filaments at the Galactic center exhibit a distinct pattern of parallelness, orientation consistency, and uniform spacing. Previous studies investigated the statistical characteristics of their orientation, finding regular patterns. This work focuses on the spacing between these filaments, analyzing their inter-filament distances to determine if they conform to either a perfect or random arrangement. By examining the probabilities associated with the observed spacing, using a Gaussian process baseline to account for potential biases, the results indicate a significant deviation from expected uniform spacing, suggesting a high-likelihood (99.9%) of these filaments being evenly spaced. This finding implies the presence of an underlying network structure.

A proposed paper suggests a new approach for a distributed optimal conservation voltage control method that focuses on reducing energy loss in unbalanced electrical distribution systems. The method aims to minimize energy loss and ensure the stability of the weak grid. It achieves this by optimizing feeder voltage to minimize power consumption and reduce branch loading. The power consumption and branch loading are described using current and power injection models. The method is implemented through a distributed optimization algorithm, which iteratively updates the optimal feeder voltage. The convergence of the method is demonstrated. A case study validates the method's ability to reduce energy loss and power quality issues, such as line overloading and reduced equipment lifespan.

We investigate non-stochastic bandits and experts in a delayed context, where delays are contingent upon both the time and arm choice. While delayed settings with time-dependent delays have been thoroughly studied, considering arm-dependent delays introduces an intricate challenge. In this paper, we first aim to establish a lower bound on regret for the bandit task. Then, we develop a new approach, inspired by the information-based method of Banachiewicz-Nash, to achieve the previously determined regret bound. The proposed method simultaneously solves for optima in both reward and delay functions, utilizing a binary search tree to compare values at relevant nodes. Subsequently, we extend our work to experts, where we show that a novel algorithm can attain an optimal regret bound of $\sqrt{NT}$, identical to the lower bound regret bound determined earlier. This algorithm is based on the arm-dependent Banachiewicz-Nash method.

Current text-generation algorithms in dialogue can be flawed, as they focus on generating grammatically correct sentences, even if they lack naturalness. To rectify this, our new framework, LEATHER, aims to produce text that sounds more human-like. By combining findings from psychological and linguistic studies, LEATHER incorporates four key factors: (1) increased use of filler words, (2) more frequent use of short sentences, (3) incorporation of common linguistic patterns and structures, and (4) greater use of vague and open-ended language. To generate text that follows these guidelines, LEATHER employs a sequence-to-sequence model that LEATHER can easily modify to generate more human-like text, and our results show that it leads to more natural-sounding dialogue compared to current methods.

Following Quantum Chromodynamics' 1972 formulation, a breakthrough in its regularization came when Kenneth Wilson applied it to Euclidean lattices. This opened doors for in-depth numerical analyses of QCD's non-perturbative features, exemplified in the initial studies by Michael Creutz. Subsequently, investigations into the QCD phase diagram and the thermodynamics of hot, dense strong-interaction matter gained significant momentum. In this concise review, some key outcomes from more than four decades of lattice QCD research on QCD thermodynamics are compiled.

A type of Gaussian process regression that accounts for epistemic uncertainty in data analysis is used in this research to create models that predict the stress in the blades and tower of offshore wind turbines. By applying a technique called chained Gaussian processes, a more accurate prediction of the stress in offshore wind turbines is achieved. This involves using a Gaussian process regression model that integrates as many as six layers of conditional distributions. The models are trained on data derived from high-fidelity simulations of offshore wind turbines under various environmental conditions. By leveraging these conditional distributions, a more accurate prediction of the stress in offshore wind turbines is achieved, particularly in situations where the models are trained on incomplete data. The results indicate that the use of chained Gaussian processes yields more reliable predictions of the stress in offshore wind turbines, particularly in the prediction of stress levels in the tower of offshore wind turbines.

Turkey is prone to seismic activities with varying intensity earthquakes occurring frequently, emphasizing the necessity for swift and effective crisis information dissemination. Social media can provide valuable insights into public perception, beneficial for crisis communication and management. This research focuses on analyzing Twitter posts related to the 2020 Izmir earthquake, aiming to leverage these insights to infer real-time public opinions.

A group G exhibits the property $R_\infty$ if all automorphisms $\varphi$ of G produce an infinite number of twisted conjugacy classes. In such cases, we determine the property $R_\infty$ for nilpotent quotients of BSd generalizations, specifically focusing on $H_{n,d}$ with n+1 being a prime number and d equal to 1 or 2. When d equals 1, we confirm that the property $R_\infty$ applies to the direct product of G and $\mathbb Z$, meaning the corresponding generalized solvable group also possesses $R_\infty$. In contrast, for d equal to 2, we demonstrate that the only automorphisms that fail to yield an infinite number of twisted conjugacy classes are those with orders two and, in cases where n is one more than a multiple of 4, four. Furthermore, we identify which orders two and four are equivalent to automorphisms of BSd and solve the problem for nilpotent quotients of BSd with the condition of being primitive.

A novel technique is developed to process time-sensitive data from ultrafast experiments using an advanced algorithm. This method builds on a traditional approach by utilizing a different data model, which incorporates information about the evolution of molecules over time. To achieve this, existing data is analyzed using a new basis, which is calculated through optimization based on the properties of molecules. This new technique allows researchers to make more accurate predictions about the molecules' behavior. It is successfully tested using experiments involving neon-like ions and is found to significantly improve understanding of these systems.

Large-scale driving datasets have significantly enhanced the development of vision-based driver assistance systems, yet current datasets have several shortcomings, primarily consisting of extracted driving scenarios from proprietary systems with limited accessibility. The available data lacks essential elements such as driving geometry and context, hindering its use in certain applications. To bridge this gap, we've introduced SceNDD, a novel dataset comprising driving scenarios with relevant information like lane detection, local map, and sensor data, all collected in a naturalistic setting using in-vehicle equipment. The dataset consists of approximately 21,973 scenarios derived from 300 hours of driving data, encompassing diverse driving behaviors, conditions, and routes in urban environments. Our paper outlines the creation process of this dataset, evaluates its characteristics, and demonstrates its potential utility in various areas, such as driver assistance and autonomous driving systems.

In connection with BCFT and ICFT, reflected entropy has been explored and discussed. As a novelty, the former focuses on the entanglement between the left and right segments of a interval in a quasi-particle framework, while the latter delves into the entanglement between a interval in a quasi-particle landscape and its mirror image. Due to its theoretical importance, the ICFT-driven contribution to reflected entropy, associated with Verma modes, has been analyzed in depth. A novel approach for computing entropy comes from a TFT-driven perspective, which is seemingly more challenging to obtain. Nonetheless, this paper proposes a method to overcome this difficulty and derives an alternative expression for reflected entropy. As a result, the TFT-driven contribution to reflected entropy can be computed using primary fields, which interestingly aligns with ICFT-driven results when primary fields' descendants are involved. These findings suggest that TFT and ICFT drive the same physical outcome, resolving a long-standing puzzle and confirming a previously proposed conjecture related to entropy's conformal dimension.

The research on Reconfigurable Intelligent Surface (RIS)-assisted Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiplexing (OFDM) systems has gained significant interest due to their potential for optimizing wireless systems. Nevertheless, the accuracy of channel estimation in these systems is crucial and heavily influenced by the length of cyclic prefix (Cyclic CUs, CUs) which might not be sufficient for their channel models. CUS do not account for the effects of hardware impairments (HIs) in the data transmission process, leading to a decline in estimation accuracy. This paper presents a novel solution to address these issues by proposing a pre-processing method based on Extreme Learning Machine (ELM) to enhance the accuracy of RIS-assisted OFDM systems. ELM is an artificial neural network type that can be used as a classifier or function approximator before or after data transmission, thus allowing for the creation of a pre-processing function to correct the effects of HIs. This paper proposes a new method called ELMP, which uses ELIM to correct the effects of HIs and increases the effective length of CUs during channel estimation. This method is capable of handling the effects of HIs and insufficient CUs in RIS-assisted OFDM systems. Our results show that the proposed system can maintain a high level of performance even when the length of CUs is reduced and HIs are present, thus allowing for the development of robust communication systems capable of handling variable lengths of CUs and HIs in RIS-ass

We are investigating a type of integral fluctuation theorem that operates independently of energy measurements, applicable across various conditions. The free particle, quantum particle, and particle subject to harmonic potential forces are examined under non-projective (projection-free) measurements. For these cases, we demonstrate that the mean energy change can be quantified through the negative reciprocal variance of the integral energy flux operator, while remaining unaffected by the system's specific potential. Additionally, we derive a unified expression for the integral flux operator applicable to any single energy measurement. By analyzing observations on both continuous variable quantum channels and free particle paths with inherent noise, we highlight the integral fluctuation theorem's utility in analyzing equilibrium and non-equilibrium conditions. Our results show that this theorem can accurately predict the thermal equilibrium state and quantify entropy production in non-equilibrium scenarios, aligning with established metrics.

We are exploring the deformations of G2-instantons on nearly G2-manifolds. A nearly G2-manifold can be viewed as a K3 surface with a 3-form that is almost compatible with its Kahler form. The almost compatibility makes it possible to consider G2-instantons that are not necessarily Hermitian-Einstein. The deformations of such G2-instantons have a complex zero-type operator and are finite-dimensional. The G2-instantons deform in a manner similar to how symplectic numbers deform under the standard deformation flow. The deformations of a G2-instanton can be equated with the holomorphic structure of the associated K3 surface. The G2-instantons deform in a manner that is equivalent to complex structures on a K3 surface. The global spread of the 2019 COVID-19 pandemic caused by SARS-CoV-2 has been rapid and widespread, leading to widespread infections and deaths. As a result, many countries have implemented a set of measures to slow the outbreak, including social distancing protocols, mass testing, and contact tracing programs. Contact tracing programs, which aim to identify individuals who have come into contact with infected persons, have become a crucial tool in controlling the spread of the virus. National contact tracing programs have been established to provide this service, with many countries developing and deploying their own contact tracing apps to facilitate contact tracing. These contact tracing apps, which are designed to provide this service, have become a central component of contact tracing programs due to their ability to identify at-risk individuals and alert them to take preventive measures. While contact tracing apps have become essential tools in controlling the outbreak, concerns have been growing over their impact on user privacy. As a result, researchers have been urging developers to ensure the privacy and security of these apps, with many solutions being proposed to address these concerns. This paper will examine the privacy of national contact tracing COVID-19 apps, with a focus on the Coronav\'irus-SUS in Brazil model, which is a well-known secure contact tracing API. A detailed analysis of this model is provided, with a discussion of its security and privacy features.

The central nervous system's underlying physiology, revealed by invasive electroencephalography, holds a secret. Beyond the surface-level macroscopic world, hidden within the data are the fundamental, tiny building blocks that govern the world - quantum components. This article presents a case for the existence of quantum information in neural systems, supported by various experimental observations, and suggests that they are the key to understanding the brain's intricate mechanisms. One potential application of this idea could be the phenomenon of brain waves during sleep, where quantum information might be used to explain the different phases. Additionally, we explore the implications of this concept for advancing both neuroscience and quantum computing research.

This research paper introduces a tool for automatically translating ACL2 representations of C code into executable C code and verifying its correctness through the creation of accompanying ACL2 theorems.

A cluster of young compact asteroids connected to 39991 Iochroma undergoes a complex dynamic evolution, influenced by perturbations. Notably, five members exhibit resonant behavior within the Iochroma group, primarily influenced by a 3:1 resonance with Iochroma. Four of these asteroids reside in a 3:1:1 three-body mean motion resonance, while another asteroid occupies a 3:2:1 resonance. This analysis involves a detailed examination of Iochroma's motion using a Hamiltonian model, incorporating its multipole field and co-orbital libration. Additionally, the motion of the other resonant asteroids in the Iochroma family is investigated, and their configurations in the plane of the sky and in 3D space are explored.

Building upon Ramanujan's well-known formula for odd zeta values, we establish a related expression using Hurwitz zeta functions. Additionally, we examine modifications to the boundary terms in Ramanujan's identity and discuss connections to the Gauss map of planar ternary cubic curves.

We calculate rational T-equivariant elliptic cohomology of complex projective spaces constructed from T-representations V of rank r ≥ 2. This is achieved by establishing that the T-equivariant elliptic cohomology theory constructed in Greenlees-Wickelgren can be expressed as a quotient of the T-equivariant cohomology of the total space of a bundle similar to the Grassmannian Gr(r,1) for the action of T, after it is imbedded into Gr(r,n) for some positive integer n > 1. This is done by demonstrating that Gr(r,n) with the T-action can be expressed as the union of two closed T-inequivalent subvarieties, each of which is homeomorphic to Gr(r,1) with the T-action, thus enabling us to apply Satake's theorem to reach this conclusion. Additionally, we verify that the rational T-equivariant elliptic cohomology of CP(V) is isomorphic to the T-equivariant cohomology of the total space of a bundle similar to the projective bundle P(V), after it is imbedded into CP(V') for some complex vector space V' of dimension r+1. Recent uses of machine learning in algebraic geometry and physics are explored,  
revealing how problems in this field can be easily translated into tensor mapping,  
a concept suitable for supervised learning, and often resulting in a training task with a large dataset.  
A brief overview is provided of relevant algebraic geometry and physical theories before discussing specific applications.  
These include an investigation of how birational geometry and duality theories affect physical relationships using entropy,  
as well as modifications to use metric moduli spaces and scale of singularities instead of algebraic ones.  
Furthermore, research into how the concept of nonperturbative supersymmetry can exist in quantum mechanics and field theory,  
and the potential for learning supersymmetry transformation from data.

This study provides a calculation to the next-to-leading order of the production process $e^{+}e^{-} \to J/\psi + (\eta_c,\chi_{c0,1,2})$ using the fixed-order perturbation theory, where the colour singlet dominant contributions for $\eta_c$ and $\chi_{cJ}$ are considered up to the $^{3}S_{1}^{[1]}$ contribution. We have determined that the angular distributions $A_{\parallel}$ and $A_{\perp}$ for $\mu_{\perp}$-integrated and total $\mu_{\perp}$-averaged distributions are influenced by higher-order QCD corrections. The calculated values of $A_{\parallel}$ and $A_{\perp}$ for $\mu_{\perp} < J/\psi$ show a difference with experimental results that are available for $J/\psi + \eta_c$. The calculated values of $k_{\perp}$ for $A_{\parallel}$ and $A_{\perp}$ for $\mu_{\perp} < J/\psi$ show a discrepancy with experimental data.
